item.title: Blanche warned of contempt risk in Epstein files case
item.description:
A federal judge warned Attorney General Todd Blanche Wednesday that he could face contempt proceedings if the Department of Justice fails to comply with an order involving the release or review of Epstein files.

Why it matters: The case could force the DOJ to release additional Epstein records or remove redactions that a court determines aren't permitted under the law.

What they're saying: U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan wrote in a 20-page order Wednesday that a civil contempt charge would be "premature" for now, but warned it could become appropriate if Blanche fails to comply with the court's renewed order.

  • "[C]ourts have the inherent power to enforce compliance with their lawful orders through civil contempt," Sullivan wrote.
  • "A contempt finding is proper where 'the putative contemnor has violated an order that is clear and unambiguous' and the violation of an order is 'proved by clear and convincing evidence.'"

The other side: "Our filings will speak for themselves," a DOJ spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • "We have already shown the Judge proof of redacted victim names and established that the plaintiff in this case seeks to unmask victim names."

Catch up quick: Independent journalist Katie Phang brought the lawsuit, alleging the DOJ hasn't released all documents required under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which Congress passed last November.

  • Sullivan said last month he didn't want to start contempt proceedings, but added that the public "has a right to know what the hell is going on in this case" and the "victims have a right to know and the court has a right to know."

Zoom in: Sullivan ruled Wednesday that the DOJ provided adequate documentation showing some email redactions were made to protect survivors' privacy.

  • But he said the department hadn't provided enough documentation to justify redactions in other emails and ordered it to provide additional documentation for private "in camera review" — a process in which a judge reviews confidential, sensitive or privileged documents outside public view.
  • The judge rejected the DOJ's assertion that handwritten FBI notes were "properly withheld because they are 'substantially similar to' and therefore duplicative of the typewritten reports." He said the DOJ's review protocol does not require withholding "substantially similar" records.
  • Sullivan also rejected the DOJ's argument for not reviewing foreign-language materials related to Epstein because it was "not practicable for a first-level reviewer to determine the responsiveness of a foreign-language document."

Yes, but: Sullivan acknowledged that some redactions covered the names and email addresses of a government attorney and law enforcement personnel, which the DOJ's review protocol requires to be redacted.

State of play: The lawsuit is one of several seeking additional transparency or alleging DOJ errors related to the Epstein files, which have generated legal and political scrutiny of the Trump administration.

  • Congress has held U.S. attorneys general in contempt before, including Eric Holder during the Obama administration and William Barr during Trump's first administration.
  • The DOJ did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

What we're watching: A House discharge petition is two signatures shy of forcing a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, which would enforce and expand the release of remaining DOJ files.

  • Outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is leading the effort, as he did with Act I.

Go deeper: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a DOJ statement.

item.title: Exclusive: Scalise puts GOP high-water mark at 225 House seats
item.description:
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) is staring at a scary political environment for Republicans and claiming to see something very different: a path to 225 seats.

Why it matters: Republican leaders insist they can retain the majority, but only if they drive their voters to the polls by manufacturing the kind of voter enthusiasm Democrats are generating organically.

  • "If we make it a contrast election, we win," Scalise told Axios in an interview Thursday.
  • "We could get to 225. It would be a good night for us if we did, but it's possible," he said.
  • "235 is not," he said. "You're literally doing coin tosses in a couple of seats."

Between the lines: Asked if he saw any signs of a blue wave forming or the map expanding, Scalise said: "Not right now. No."

Reality check: Republicans know that history — and many of the indicators heading into November — is working against them.

  • "I know what history says, you know, but history's not on the ballot," Scalise said.
  • Still, Democrats are turning out in primaries — and special elections — as if they're getting free gas cards for showing up.

Democrats lead by nearly nine percentage points on the generic ballot.

  • President Trump's approval rating is below 40%, according to the RealClearPolitics average.
  • And Trump is underwater by a whopping 61 percentage points on inflation in a recent poll, an apparent record.

Zoom in: Republicans are examining the map with a jeweler's loupe and insist the picture isn't as bleak in the pivotal battleground seats.

  • "We're not looking at national polls; we go district by district," Scalise said.
  • That means trench warfare in 35 seats, where Republicans say they have proven winners, plenty of money and new rules to spend it.
  • "We've got 20 [seats] on our side that we're fighting to hold on to that are real competitive, and 15 [seats] that we have a real chance to flip," he said. "These are knock-down, drag-out fights."

What we're hearing: The White House has long thought of the midterms as a "hate election." Scalise uses the more genteel term "contrast election."

  • But before Republicans can dream about growing their majority, they need to fix their enthusiasm problem — and match the Democratic energy showing up in many of the preelection indicators.

The GOP's midterm convention in Dallas last week was the first step.

  • "If we are able to capitalize on that kind of enthusiasm and carry that momentum into November, then we'll have the same turnout as the other side, and we'll hold the majority," Scalise said.
  • Now comes the road show: Congressional leaders — and the president — are hitting the campaign trail.
  • In the next two weeks, Scalise will travel to 11 states to campaign for 16 Republicans — incumbents and challengers.

The bottom line: The 225-seat scenario is Scalise's high-water mark. At another point in the interview, he suggested the majority could be smaller — closer to the 220–215 split Republicans won in 2024.

  • "This isn't going to be a 10-seat majority, but it could be a six-seat majority."

item.title: Scoop: Trump expected to meet with Venezuela's new leader
item.description:
President Trump is making plans for a first-ever meeting with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, as early as next week, sources familiar with the discussions tell Axios.

Why it matters: The potential meeting showcases the close relations between the nations under Trump. But it's also fraught with political risks that extend from Miami to Caracas.

Driving the news: Trump is already planning to meet with Gulf leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York next week to discuss the Iran War, and those who know his thinking say he wants to make time for a sidelines sit-down with Rodriguez as early as Tuesday, sources said.

  • "Iran is tough, but Venezuela is without a doubt the president's top success and Delcy is a key to that," a Trump adviser said. "Unless something goes really wrong, the president wants to make time."
  • A senior administration official cautioned: "Nothing is finalized. This is up to the president."
  • On Sunday, when asked about meeting Rodriguez, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that "I may be, I may be."

Zoom in: The New York City meeting could happen just blocks from the federal lockup where Rodriguez's predecessor and onetime ally, socialist Nicolas Maduro, awaits trial on narco-terrorism charges.

  • Maduro was seized Jan. 3 in Caracas in a U.S. military operation authorized by Trump.
  • Rodriguez assumed power after the coup and has worked closely with Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to normalize relations between the countries, including the inking of a massive but controversial Venezuelan oil deal first reported by Axios.

Friction point: Clustered in South Florida, conservative and vocal Venezuelan exile community has expressed increasing agitation with the administration for working so closely with Rodriguez, a lifelong socialist who rose to power along with Maduro under strongman Hugo Chavez, both foes of the U.S. this century.

  • Adding to the anger in the diaspora: neither Trump nor Rubio has called for elections in Venezuela, despite years of bashing Maduro as an election-stealing dictator.
  • Supporters of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado also grew frustrated with administration officials over their criticism of the exiled Venezuelan political leader when she tried to return home after the earthquakes in June.

The big picture: In Florrida, politicians, pollsters and consultants say higher gas prices due to the Iran war and the administration's heavy-handed immigration enforcement are bigger political problems for Republicans in the midterm elections than promoting democracy now in Venezuela.

  • Polls in Venezuela show Rodriguez and Trump have low favorability ratings and Machado has the highest, although it's declining.
  • Some in Trump's orbit have expressed concern that the optics of a meeting with Trump will hurt Rodriguez even more at home because she could look like too much of a U.S. puppet.
  • But Trump isn't concerned about that, the administration official said, noting "The fact is POTUS loves Delcy because she's delivering and she's leading."

item.title: Inside House Democrats' behind-the-scenes food fight
item.description:
The House's last in-session week before the midterms was beset by furious private finger-pointing between House Democrats following several high-profile rebellions.

Why it matters: This dynamic may only worsen if Democrats retake the House, which is set to see an influx of distinctly rebellious and independent lawmakers, particularly on the left.

  • There is even chatter among members contrasting the ability of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to control members with that of his top deputy, Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), according to two House Democrats.
  • Said one of the lawmakers, speaking on the condition of anonymity to share details of sensitive private discussions: "People are talking about 'mom and dad'. … Dad is soft."
  • "I think people are asking the question: If this is happening in the minority, are you prepared for what will happen in the majority?" said a third House Democrat.

"There is no daylight between the three of us," Jeffries said at a Thursday press conference with Clark and Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.).

  • "We'll address the situation when we address the situation," he added.
  • A Democratic leadership aide told Axios that everything Jeffries' deputies do is in coordination with him and doesn't represent a break between leaders.

Driving the news: Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Jared Golden (D-Maine) on Tuesday provided Republican leadership with the necessary votes to advance a package of GOP bills, including a Russia sanctions bill strongly opposed by Democratic leaders.

  • It was the second time this month the pair of centrists defected from leadership on a procedural vote — even after Clark and Jeffries publicly threatened them with punishment the first time.
  • "People thought the first time was a mistake. The second time is defiance," said a fourth House Democrat, telling Axios the two "operate like they are above the caucus."
  • Clark, along with Jeffries, engaged Gluesenkamp Perez in a heated discussion on the House floor during the vote in view of an Axios reporter, which sources said was about her defection.

The rebellion came after Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) forced a vote on impeaching President Trump without support from leadership.

  • The vote angered many House Democrats, who complained Green was muddying the party's message on a crucial week.
  • Jeffries and Clark voted "present" along with 44 other Democrats. 147 sided with Green and 18 voted with Republicans to quash the impeachment effort.
  • Leadership's neutrality on that vote drew frustration as well, with a fifth House Democrat telling Axios: "Our constituents don't send us here to be 'present.' They send us here to use our judgment."

What they're saying: OurRevolution executive director Joseph Geevarghese said Jeffries "never seems to have this much trouble figuring out what to do when progressives are in his sights."

  • "You cannot demand discipline from progressives while treating defections to the right as an unsolvable procedural dilemma," he told Axios.
  • Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-N.J.) said progressives "catch shit" for being "too ideologic and bold on our ideas," and that it's "curious ... how there isn't an equally vocal attack" on centrists who break from the party line.
  • Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for the left-wing Justice Democrats: "Leadership is threatening a Democratic majority in November by refusing to stand up to the corporate Democrats aiding and abetting Republicans' agenda."

What we're hearing: Jeffries isn't the only target of rank-and-file backlash — Clark is getting heat from moderates for taking a swipe at Gluesenkamp Perez.

  • The minority whip told reporters Wednesday that "it's team players who should sit on exclusive committees," which was widely interpreted as a reference to Gluesenkamp Perez's seat on the Appropriations Committee.
  • Fumed a sixth House Democrat: "Katherine Clark just declared on moderate Democrats, which is a risky move for leadership going into a potentially tight majority."
  • Jeffries' has been far more muted, repeatedly saying he will "have more to say about the situation when I have more to say about the situation."

Much of the fury is also directed at Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, with some of it is coming from their fellow centrists.

  • "Everyone in the caucus is sick of the bullshit. Everyone has their ... number," a seventh House Democrat, a moderate, told Axios.
  • "Marie is playing with fire," a senior House Democrat told Axios, adding that Jeffries "may not do anything now, but her committee appointment may be in jeopardy for next session."

The other side: Gluesenkamp Perez said in a statement to Axios, "I don't worry about that kind of stuff. I will always vote my District and let others play inside DC politics games."

  • Said Golden: "I'm a Mainer and an American. I'm also a proud Democrat, but that team is a distant third."

The bottom line: "Members have concerns about those who are not team players," a ninth House Democrat told Axios, and "next year is the best time to address it."

  • Golden, who is retiring, has a warning for his colleagues: "Be careful what you wish for. Next time, it could be you facing punishment for putting your constituency or our country ahead of the party."

item.title: RFK Jr. questions vaccine safety at anti-vaccine organization gathering
item.description:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday returned to the the anti-vaccine group he founded, using a keynote address to signal the Trump administration isn't done questioning the safety of routine shots and expanding carveouts to federal mandates.

Why it matters: Though Kennedy avoided some of his most politically incendiary rhetoric, the speech made clear that the Department of Health and Human Services is working hard behind the scenes to continue reshaping federal vaccine policy.

  • He again questioned the safety of routine childhood vaccines and asserted they play a role in the development of chronic illnesses — questions that ignore decades of science supporting the vaccines' safety.

Driving the news: Kennedy spoke for more than an hour Thursday afternoon at a Children's Health Defense meeting in Washington, D.C., highlighting the Trump administration's work on healthy food before turning to vaccines.

  • He listed what the federal government is doing to reverse, in vaccine critics' eyes, decades of negligence on the issue.
  • And Kennedy assured the audience that President Trump is fully committed to the cause.
  • "He's directed us to pursue answers to strengthen vaccine safety, to expand options for families who want them and to preserve individual choice without federal mandates," Kennedy said. "Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House."

Between the lines: Kennedy addressed those frustrated with the administration's pace, in a nod to Make America Healthy Again movement members who feel he hasn't done enough to crack down on vaccines.

  • "In government, a bunch of things have to happen before something else happens, or you get sued, and it's a very laborious system, and there's a lot of inertia built in," he said.
  • "If we were able to overcome it, we would have changed things on day one, but those would have been short lived and I would have been out of a job."

He certainly didn't sound like someone who's ready to leave office after the midterm elections, as has been rumored.

  • The backing he appears to have from Trump himself reinforces that.
  • "I didn't come to Washington to protect institutions from uncomfortable questions," he said. "I came to make those institutions answer those questions, and I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able."

Reality check: The vast majority of health experts and scientists say that the question of vaccine safety is settled, pointing to reams of evidence accumulated over many years.

  • "It's a complete fabrication, because there's been so much data on vaccine safety," said Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security and spokesperson for the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
  • "But the overarching point is no matter how much evidence there is or that accumulates, it will not change RFK Jr.'s mind related to vaccines."

The big picture: A pre-midterm pause on Kennedy's vaccine rhetoric ended weeks ago, when he stood with the president as Trump signed an executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations, splitting the childhood MMR vaccine into three shots and delivering vaccines at separate medical visits.

  • Kennedy's speech mentioned numerous ongoing efforts within HHS to study vaccine safety, "including cumulative effects, longer-term health outcomes, uses of adjuvants, the safety of adjuvants, and many, many other issues."
  • Researchers are also also "examining questions involving adjuvants, timing, vaccination during pregnancy, maternal immunity, timing and a range of health outcomes, from allergies to autoimmune diseases to autism and other neurodevelopmental disorders," he added.

The bottom line: Expect, at a minimum, results of Kennedy-requested vaccine safety studies to come out of HHS in the second half of Trump's term.

  • Experts aren't expecting those studies to meet high scientific standards.
  • "Anything RFK Jr. touches, I'm not confident of it's veracity," Adalja said. "I have zero confidence in anything that comes from his department."
item.content:encoded:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday returned to the the anti-vaccine group he founded, using a keynote address to signal the Trump administration isn't done questioning the safety of routine shots and expanding carveouts to federal mandates.

Why it matters: Though Kennedy avoided some of his most politically incendiary rhetoric, the speech made clear that the Department of Health and Human Services is working hard behind the scenes to continue reshaping federal vaccine policy.

  • He again questioned the safety of routine childhood vaccines and asserted they play a role in the development of chronic illnesses — questions that ignore decades of science supporting the vaccines' safety.

Driving the news: Kennedy spoke for more than an hour Thursday afternoon at a Children's Health Defense meeting in Washington, D.C., highlighting the Trump administration's work on healthy food before turning to vaccines.

  • He listed what the federal government is doing to reverse, in vaccine critics' eyes, decades of negligence on the issue.
  • And Kennedy assured the audience that President Trump is fully committed to the cause.
  • "He's directed us to pursue answers to strengthen vaccine safety, to expand options for families who want them and to preserve individual choice without federal mandates," Kennedy said. "Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House."

Between the lines: Kennedy addressed those frustrated with the administration's pace, in a nod to Make America Healthy Again movement members who feel he hasn't done enough to crack down on vaccines.

  • "In government, a bunch of things have to happen before something else happens, or you get sued, and it's a very laborious system, and there's a lot of inertia built in," he said.
  • "If we were able to overcome it, we would have changed things on day one, but those would have been short lived and I would have been out of a job."

He certainly didn't sound like someone who's ready to leave office after the midterm elections, as has been rumored.

  • The backing he appears to have from Trump himself reinforces that.
  • "I didn't come to Washington to protect institutions from uncomfortable questions," he said. "I came to make those institutions answer those questions, and I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able."

Reality check: The vast majority of health experts and scientists say that the question of vaccine safety is settled, pointing to reams of evidence accumulated over many years.

  • "It's a complete fabrication, because there's been so much data on vaccine safety," said Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security and spokesperson for the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
  • "But the overarching point is no matter how much evidence there is or that accumulates, it will not change RFK Jr.'s mind related to vaccines."

The big picture: A pre-midterm pause on Kennedy's vaccine rhetoric ended weeks ago, when he stood with the president as Trump signed an executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations, splitting the childhood MMR vaccine into three shots and delivering vaccines at separate medical visits.

  • Kennedy's speech mentioned numerous ongoing efforts within HHS to study vaccine safety, "including cumulative effects, longer-term health outcomes, uses of adjuvants, the safety of adjuvants, and many, many other issues."
  • Researchers are also also "examining questions involving adjuvants, timing, vaccination during pregnancy, maternal immunity, timing and a range of health outcomes, from allergies to autoimmune diseases to autism and other neurodevelopmental disorders," he added.

The bottom line: Expect, at a minimum, results of Kennedy-requested vaccine safety studies to come out of HHS in the second half of Trump's term.

  • Experts aren't expecting those studies to meet high scientific standards.
  • "Anything RFK Jr. touches, I'm not confident of it's veracity," Adalja said. "I have zero confidence in anything that comes from his department."

item.title: Judge steps in as Kennedy Center demolition fears grow
item.description:
Trump officials must give 30 days' written notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center "including but not limited to any 'demolition'" of the main building, a federal judge ruled Thursday.

Why it matters: The ruling reinforces an earlier injunction blocking the Kennedy Center from closing for its planned renovation, after President Trump and administration officials raised the possibility of demolishing the building.

  • The ruling allows the center to continue to make "emergency repairs" rather than halt them entirely.

Driving the news: District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled Thursday that the defendants must file a "detailed status report, supported by a sworn declaration from a knowledgeable representative of the Kennedy Center, on the 'temporary closure' and emergency repairs described" in the Kennedy Center board's most recent court filing, per a minute order published Thursday.

  • Representatives for the White House and Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Catch up quick: Trump said on social media Tuesday that the center was going to be closed.

  • Shortly after, an announcement played over the center's loudspeakers telling attendees that it was closed. Legal counsel for the institution initially said someone had improperly triggered a fire alarm, causing the loudspeaker announcement.
  • But when the plaintiff's staff attempted to enter Wednesday during regular operating hours, security denied them entry and said the building was closed for interior construction and safety reasons.
  • The staff member said she later saw workers using forklifts to bring in additional construction-style gates and watched a forklift carrying permanent fencing repeatedly strike the building's structural pillars.

Context: Trump was recently pictured looking at a markup reading, "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED."

  • He told reporters on Wednesday that the Kennedy Center had been bleeding money before he "got involved."
  • "For the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term, and to carry it, or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition."
  • "Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape. ... You see steel falling down. You see plaster falling off ceilings. ... It's been very badly maintained for 25 years."

Zoom in: Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) has been in a legal battle with the administration since the center's board, made up of Trump appointees, began making changes, including adding the president's name to the building's facade.

  • Judge Cooper has repeatedly blocked that move, determining that only Congress can change the building's name and that even a small inscription would violate the legislation that christened the building.
  • Trump subsequently announced that the center would close.

State of play: Beatty's legal team says it is unclear what construction is underway and has raised concerns that the center could undertake demolition or other work that would make public access impossible and circumvent the court's order.

  • The previous injunction doesn't prevent the center from undertaking renovations and repairs without shutting down.
  • But Beatty's attorneys say, "the nature of the construction activities and any potential demolition are unclear. Given the unexplained and unlawful closure, it is possible Defendants intend to undertake immediate steps in order to make public access practically impossible for the foreseeable future," the filing reads.

Go deeper: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Fear and loathing in Trump's Miami backyard over immigration crackdown
item.description:
Staring into the camera, Rep. Maria Salazar cut a new campaign ad that told President Trump what so many of her fellow Hispanic Republicans in Miami are saying: Immigration crackdown has gone too far.

Why it matters: The anger at Trump over heavy-handed immigration enforcement is palpable in Miami-Dade County, and there's mounting political worry among Republicans across the state that it could cost the GOP in the midterm elections.

Zoom in: A bellwether, Miami-Dade is Florida's most-populous county, which Trump flipped to the Republican column in 2020 and 2024 thanks to strong Latino support, especially among Cuban Americans.

  • "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in her ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
  • Trump carried her district by 15 points two years ago. Today, she's tied in polls with newscaster Eliot Rodriguez, a fellow Cuban American, who said her new ad was a sign of desperation.
  • A Trump adviser told Axios: "I'm getting the Trumpiest Cubans sending me videos from Miami of guys getting busted at places like the gas station, for no apparent reason."

By the numbers: In Miami-Dade, 62% of the county's 1.3 million registered voters are Hispanic. They account for 76% of the registered Republicans.

  • 63% of Hispanic voters said they supported "deporting illegal immigrants" while 34% were opposed to them, according to a poll conducted last month by a GOP pollster and shared with Axios
  • But those numbers switched when it came to how deportations were being carried out: Just 29% were in favor; 58% were opposed.
  • "The support is just evaporating. The economy sucks and ICE is just out of control," said the pollster, who's from Miami. "People feel they didn't sign up for this."

Yes, but: Trump ran on a platform of mass deportations. He promised to target undocumented criminals, but the president's critics warned that his aggressive immigration push would lead to raids, arrests in the streets, racial profiling and separated families.

  • "There was truth in advertising," the pollster said.
  • Trump last year also began revoking Temporary Protected Status for as many as 1.3 million people across the country, some of whom first received the TPS designation in 1998.
  • "Temporary means temporary," a White House official told Axios, noting that President Biden had allowed millions into the country under TPS and a new program that Trump reversed.

Ground zero for the Miami-Dade fear and loathing is in Doral. Trump owns a prized golf course there. It's also nicknamed "Doralzuela" because of the large Venezuelan population.

  • Businesses were hit doubly hard last year when Trump canceled TPS for Venezuelans: Legal workers lost the authorization to work, once-legal residents fled, and those who are still there are in hiding or constantly getting picked up by federal agents.
  • "Our sales have dropped 70%. We spend hours empty," Katia Rios of Pipo Burgers, told CBS Miami on Wednesday.
  • Doral Mayor Christi Fraga, a Republican, has been besieged with complaints and has tried to distance herself from the Trump administration. "I don't agree with the way things are handled," she told CBS.

Zoom out: Salazar's Republican congressional colleague from Miami, Mario Diaz-Balart, has a district that stretches from Doral on Florida's southeast coast to Naples on its southwest coast.

  • "We've been sending this message to the administration for months," he said of Salazar's ad. Diaz-Balart, however, hasn't spoken publicly against the administration because he prefers to work behind the scenes.
  • Republicans say they're not too worried about conservative Hispanic voters switching to vote for Democrats, but they all believe turnout for the GOP will be low, which could affect legislative and congressional contests, and perhaps the race for governor.
  • "Byron Donalds better watch out," a top Republican consultant said of the Republican congressman locked in a tighter-than-expected gubernatorial race against Democrat David Jolly. (A Donalds spokesman said Jolly will lose.)

Friction point: Miami's best-known Cuban American political figure, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has been publicly supportive of the administration's immigration policies, despite the outcry back home.

  • Rubio was identified with bipartisan immigration reform in 2013, when he served in the Senate.
  • Venezuelans have grown increasingly agitated with Rubio and Trump for not voicing support for an election date in Venezuela and for the administration's transactional relationship with its acting president, Delcy Rodriguez, a socialist who came to power after the U.S. ousted strongman Nicolas Maduro on Jan. 3.
  • "There's a growing feeling that Trump just wanted our oil," a Venezuelan Republican activist said.

Between the lines: Miami-Dade has one of the country's most-diverse Latino populations. Cuban Americans are the dominant group, but there are sizable communities with roots elsewhere in Latin America.

  • Cuban Americans tend to be the most conservative because of the exile community that swelled after Fidel Castro took power there in the 1959 revolution.
  • Exiles from families who fled leftist oppression or violence in Nicaragua, Colombia and Venezuela also found common cause with Cuban-American Republicans over the years.
  • Now, these South Florida Hispanic communities are grappling with an immigration system that treats them about the same as Haitians in Miami or arrivals from Mexico in more liberal U.S. cities such as Los Angeles.

Cubans once enjoyed expansive immigration protections in the U.S.

  • Under Trump, they're being deported in large numbers to Mexico and even countries in Africa.

Behind the scenes: Salazar's broadside against Trump followed days of discussions between her office, Diaz-Balart's and the administration over the arrest of Luis Galeano, a Nicaraguan journalist in Miami with an active asylum application.

  • The Department of Homeland Security accused Galeano of overstaying his visa.
  • The lawmakers say his visa should have been paused because of his asylum claim, which stemmed from his critical coverage of Nicaragua's leftist dictator, Daniel Ortega, who confiscated Galeano's property and stripped him of Nicaraguan citizenship.
  • "There has got to be a better way to do this," Diaz-Balart said. "I'm hearing that everywhere."

item.title: UN mission finds reasonable grounds to believe U.S. committed war crimes in Iran
item.description:
The U.S. may have committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran, including a mass-casualty strike on a school for which Washington has yet to claim responsibility, a UN fact-finding mission said in a report released Thursday.

The big picture: The administration has waged a campaign of aggressive, norm-busting war-fighting, with the president repeatedly threatening to hit civilian infrastructure in his pressure campaign on Tehran.

  • The president has shrugged off questions about his attacks on Iran and previously said he wasn't concerned if his threats could amount to war crimes.
  • The White House and Pentagon did not immediately respond to Axios' request to respond to the UN team's findings.

What's inside: The UN mission found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. carried out the Feb. 28 strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in southern Iran that a count cited in the report said killed more than 120 children.

  • Back in May, U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper told the House Armed Services Committee the Minab attack "correlated" with a U.S. strike. And in June, President Trump said "nobody did that on purpose" and that "mistakes are made."
  • The UN team found reasonable grounds to believe the U.S. carried out both the school strike and another on a sports center. Both, the UN report said, amount to war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack.
  • CENTCOM has denied carrying out the sports center attack.

What they're saying: The "U.S. failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective," the mission's report said of the school strike.

  • The mission sought information on the strikes and attempted to meet with U.S. officials but received no response, the report said.

Zoom out: The report further detailed "gross human rights violations" committed by Iran, including those that breached freedom from torture, fair trial and the right to freely assemble, among others.

  • It said Iran has announced at least 58 executions since the start of 2026, including 29 men executed in connection with the mass 2025–2026 protests.
  • It also concluded the nationwide internet shutdown and communications restrictions unduly restricted the right to seek and receive information.
  • "Many gross human rights violations by Iran amount to the crimes against humanity of murder, imprisonment and other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, and other inhumane acts," it read.

What we're watching: The findings come days before world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly's annual general debate, which begins Tuesday.

Go deeper: Scoop: Trump to hold Iran talks with Gulf leaders next week

item.title: White House pulls ICE nominee who drew MAGA pushback
item.description:
The White House is pulling Lance Schroyer's stalled nomination to lead ICE.

The big picture: Schroyer's limited immigration experience created tension between Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and border czar Tom Homan, along with other MAGA figures, Axios' Brittany Gibson reported last month.

Driving the news: The White House did not explain why it withdrew the nomination of Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state highway trooper.

  • Schroyer was also formerly part of Mullin's security detail.

Catch up quick: Trump announced Schroyer's nomination in June, saying he "has what it takes to DETAIN AND DEPORT Illegal Alien Criminals."

  • He urged the Senate to "CONFIRM Lance, IMMEDIATELY" — but that didn't happen.
  • David Venturella, who previously worked for a private prison operator, is the current acting ICE director.

Friction point: Schroyer would've taken over a multi-billion dollar budget, inflated under the Trump administration, and a sprawling immigration crackdown that's triggered mass protests, lawsuits and due process concerns.

  • Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) threatened to delay Schroyer's confirmation hearing until he received more information about the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota earlier this year, The Wall Street Journal reported last month.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Trump tells Axios he's approaching major crossroads in Iran war
item.description:
President Trump told Axios Thursday that he's approaching a critical juncture in the Iran war over whether to restart massive attacks in an effort to bring the conflict to a close.

  • "I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me."

Why it matters: Though Trump has made similar threats before, his comments come ahead of a planned meeting Tuesday with leaders from six Gulf countries — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman — on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

  • The meeting could shape the next phase of the war, including whether to make another push for diplomacy or intensify military action. If Trump wants to resume major combat operations, he would need buy-in from his regional allies.
  • The president has said several times in recent days that the war will end soon. Some U.S. officials warn that the conflict has settled into an unsustainable, neither-war-nor-peace stalemate, and they believe Trump could return to major combat operations after the midterms if a deal isn't reached by then.

What he's saying: Trump made clear in the interview that he wants to use the meeting at the UN to hear directly from regional allies about the war's next steps.

  • "I want to find out where they are and how they are doing. We have been very protective of them," Trump said.
  • Trump declined to say whether he'll decide on the path forward before or after the midterms.

Driving the news: In early August, Trump held off on resuming major combat operations after Saudi Arabia and Qatar expressed concern that Iran would bomb Saudi oil and gas facilities in retaliation.

  • Since then, Trump has taken a "low-key" approach: suspending negotiations with Iran, launching a new economic sanctions campaign, continuing a naval blockade on Iranian ports, and focusing the U.S. military on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and increasing oil flow to the global energy market.
  • The U.S. military has significantly increased oil and gas tanker transit through the strait. But traffic is still below pre-war levels, and oil prices remain high.

State of play: Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have ordered the military to maintain its level of forces in the Middle East until the end of the year, U.S. officials say, to remain ready for a potential return to full-scale combat.

  • The officials say Trump needs to decide soon on the way forward, partly because the U.S. military can't stay in its current holding pattern much longer. "At some point, you have to decide what is the endgame," one of the officials said.
  • Trump told Axios he's very satisfied that the naval blockade has prevented Iran from exporting its oil. "Not one ship has gone to Iran since we started. They tried and we blew them up," he said.
  • The president added that Iran is in direct contact with the U.S. and said the Iranians still want to reach a deal.

The big picture: The White House has also been working on a post-war strategy that calls for a regional effort to contain Iran while expanding normalization of relations between Israel and its neighbors.

  • While the plan is still in the early stages of drafting, it's intended to guide the U.S. approach in the Middle East after the Iran war ends and in the final two years of Trump's term. Two big events loom over the planning: the Oct. 27 election in Israel and the U.S. midterms in November.

What to watch: When asked if he will meet with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in New York next week, Trump said, "I may."
item.content:encoded:
President Trump told Axios Thursday that he's approaching a critical juncture in the Iran war over whether to restart massive attacks in an effort to bring the conflict to a close.

  • "I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me."

Why it matters: Though Trump has made similar threats before, his comments come ahead of a planned meeting Tuesday with leaders from six Gulf countries — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman — on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

  • The meeting could shape the next phase of the war, including whether to make another push for diplomacy or intensify military action. If Trump wants to resume major combat operations, he would need buy-in from his regional allies.
  • The president has said several times in recent days that the war will end soon. Some U.S. officials warn that the conflict has settled into an unsustainable, neither-war-nor-peace stalemate, and they believe Trump could return to major combat operations after the midterms if a deal isn't reached by then.

What he's saying: Trump made clear in the interview that he wants to use the meeting at the UN to hear directly from regional allies about the war's next steps.

  • "I want to find out where they are and how they are doing. We have been very protective of them," Trump said.
  • Trump declined to say whether he'll decide on the path forward before or after the midterms.

Driving the news: In early August, Trump held off on resuming major combat operations after Saudi Arabia and Qatar expressed concern that Iran would bomb Saudi oil and gas facilities in retaliation.

  • Since then, Trump has taken a "low-key" approach: suspending negotiations with Iran, launching a new economic sanctions campaign, continuing a naval blockade on Iranian ports, and focusing the U.S. military on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and increasing oil flow to the global energy market.

item.title: States prep for ICE agents to be at polls, just in case
item.description:
The Trump administration's hints about sending ICE agents to election polling places this fall have led state officials from Maine to Oregon to make plans to counter any actions that could affect voters.

Why it matters: It's illegal for federal law enforcement to be at polling places — and there are limits on how close local authorities can be — but when asked about ICE at the polls, President Trump said in May he'd "do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections."

  • Earlier this month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE agents could be at polling places if they were serving an immigration warrant.
  • "We would be engaging in malpractice if we didn't prepare for the concern [about ICE agents showing up at polls] and we didn't address it," New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver told Axios.

The big picture: State election officials nationwide told Axios how they're working with local election officials and state attorneys general to prep for the possibility of ICE disrupting voting or ballot drop box operations.

  • "ICE doesn't have a role here," said Aghogho Edevbie, Michigan's deputy secretary of state. "Certainly any ICE activity near a polling location can be considered voter intimidation, and we would take steps to counter that immediately."

Zoom in: Toulouse Oliver said her office's preparations for any federal agents are similar to how it would deal with other unauthorized people at the polls.

  • Her office is training local election officials to initially ask any officers to leave the voting area. If necessary, then they should call the county sheriff. The next step would be legal action against any unauthorized people.
  • "An ICE agent is the same as any other unauthorized individual at a polling location, and the same protocols should be followed," she said.

What they're saying: "If the Trump administration were to go down that path, the individuals involved would be committing crimes," Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said, describing a similar protocol in her state.

  • "The coordination between secretaries of state, clerks, attorneys general, and partners at every level is very close," she added.

Zoom out: Election officials typically respond to myriad disruptions during election season.

  • Bellows told Axios she has dealt with several cases of "swatting" at polling places, referring to when someone calls in a fake emergency to a location to try to interrupt voting.
  • In Oregon, Secretary of State Tobias Read compared preparing for ICE agents to dealing with major wildfires during a past election season.
  • "Our system has to deal with all kinds of disasters, not just manufactured ones like the one from the White House right now," Read said.

Colorado's secretary of state, Jena Griswold, has experience responding to a case of potential voter intimidation in 2020, when two observers who were openly carrying weapons began filming people at the polls. The men eventually left the area after prompting from local officials, and weren't charged.

  • The city of Denver, a major target for Trump's immigration crackdown, is involved in litigation aimed at preemptively blocking ICE agents from showing up at the polls.

Between the lines: Mullin's recent statements that ICE agents will be at polling places only if they're making a targeted arrest haven't reassured election officials.

  • "I think people could look to Minnesota and the fact that Alex Pretti and Ms. [Renée] Good are dead to talk about ICE's effectiveness and the appropriateness of their action," Read said.

The other side: "America's elections are NOT a sanctuary from federal criminal law, and [the Department of Homeland Security] will not pretend otherwise because a secretary of state held a training," a DHS spokesperson told Axios in a statement.

  • "ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action."

DHS used to have a more robust partnership to help secure elections from physical and digital threats, through the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

  • But the Trump administration has made significant cuts to that agency, and some of the regional offices that handled that work are now empty.

item.title: Hasan Piker on "The Axios Show": America worse than al-Qaeda "pound for pound"
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker tells Axios he believes America conducts more terrorism in the world than al-Qaeda, the terror network that carried out the 9/11 attacks.

  • "Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker said in an exclusive interview for a new episode of "The Axios Show." Piker added: "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world."

Why it matters: Piker is one of the most popular streamers on Twitch, and his history of incendiary statements has become central to Republicans' attacks in the critical Senate race in Michigan since Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed had Piker campaign for him in the primary.

Driving the news: Piker's comments to Axios came in response to a question about his previous statement that "America is the top dog in terrorism."

  • Piker pointed to the deaths of more than 100 people at an elementary school in Minab, Iran, earlier this year. The AP found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school.
  • "If you're killing 140 schoolgirls, that is an act of terror," he said. "This doesn't mean that all Americans are terrorists, but the reality of the matter is we have to create an environment of accountability to ensure things like that never happen again."
  • The Trump administration has not yet released findings from a Pentagon investigation, and an exact death toll is not known.

The big picture: Republican-affiliated groups already have spent nearly $3 million in ads attacking El-Sayed over his affiliation with Piker, according to the tracking firm AdImpact.

  • Most of the ads feature a clip of Piker in 2019 saying that "America deserved 9/11." He apologized for the remark and has since argued that the terror attacks were part of "blowback" from U.S. involvement in the Middle East in previous decades.
  • "This doesn't justify the action, mind you," he told Axios. "This is more so analysis to stop further violence from taking place, both violence in the region, but also violence in the home front as well."

Michigan's GOP Senate nominee, Mike Rogers, also frequently ties Piker to El-Sayed.

  • In his speech at the recent Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Rogers said: "Abdul El-Sayed has chosen Hasan as his running mate. Together, they attack America, excuse extremism, and treat our country like the villain."

El-Sayed has largely dodged questions about Piker and occasionally appeared irritated by them, often referring to him as just a "streamer in California."

  • "The reason I talk to Hasan isn't because of Hasan, it's because of the 3 million people who pay attention to what he has to say," El-Sayed told Fox 2 Detroit Tuesday night at a debate where Rogers didn't show up.
  • "Too often the way that our politics happen is that we're told who we cannot talk to," El-Sayed added.

In a statement to Axios on Wednesday, El-Sayed said, "I do not agree with this statement [on al-Qaeda], nor do I give much weight to the statements made by a social media streamer. I am more concerned with the dangerous policies of Donald Trump and Mike Rogers that are raising the prices of gas, groceries and healthcare for Michiganders."

item.title: AI's imminent hacking threat is hiding in plain sight
item.description:
An unprecedented wave of AI-powered, human-driven cyberattacks is coming, security experts say — and it's a far more urgent risk than theoretical conversations about AI wiping out humanity.

Why it matters: The great September AI panic — which spread from boardrooms to Congress to American households in the last week — may have missed the point.

  • Powerful models with advanced cybersecurity capabilities are already allowing attackers to bypass the human bottleneck that has long prevented most hacking campaigns from reaching industrial scale.
  • Executives and former officials have told Axios they fear automated cyberattacks that turn off critical services like the power grid, or attackers using AI agents (like the ones that breached Hugging Face) to hack self-driving cars or create a botnet that takes over the whole internet.

Driving the news: OpenAI on Wednesday disclosed six new incidents in which its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials, uploaded files to the public internet or communicated across supposedly isolated training environments.

The big picture: Rather than seeing recent safety failures at OpenAI and other frontier labs as terrifying instances of agents running amok, seasoned cybersecurity experts instead say they represent cautionary tales illustrating what will happen when powerful models meet poor security controls.

  • "The more we have been peeking under the hood to understand exactly what happened, the more we realize that there was a lot of human error in the picture," Michele Catasta, the president and head of AI at app builder Replit, told Axios.

For the record: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said the Hugging Face breach was the "first security incident that I have felt very viscerally," and the company has implemented new internal controls.

  • Kai Chen, alignment research lead at OpenAI, told Axios in an interview Wednesday that the safety incidents they've faced are both due to internal systems and advancing model capabilities.
  • "It's true that model capabilities have grown faster than we expected, but there are also things internally that we can change and improve," Chen said. "We need to step up to meet this new era of AI development, and voluntary disclosures should be a part of that."

Between the lines: Catasta and others who spoke at an Imagination in Action event at Google's headquarters Monday offered a view that the imminent threat from cyber intrusions is formidable.

  • "I don't worry about the machine waking up and deciding to end us," Bugcrowd CEO Dave Gerry told Axios. "What I worry about is a system with too much access doing exactly what it was told without the necessary adversarial testing."
  • Mimecast CEO Ranjan Singh told Axios that the real risk is happening today with AI agents that have access to sensitive documents and internal corporate systems.
  • "It is right to sound the alarm, but the risk doesn't require an internet-scale swarm to become real," he said. "Most organizations can't tell you who or what that agent is, what it's allowed to touch, or who's accountable when it does something it shouldn't."

What to watch: A number of business executives are saying behind closed doors that they plan to hold frontier labs accountable for the behavior of their models. If they get hacked as Hugging Face did, expect litigation.

  • A senior executive at a top hedge fund who spoke to Axios said his first call, if his firm had suffered a similar attack, would be to his general counsel to prepare a lawsuit.

Go deeper: Humans are leaving the door wide open for AI hacking

item.title: Scoop: Trump to hold Iran talks with Gulf leaders next week
item.description:
President Trump is expected to hold a meeting with Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the war with Iran, three sources with direct knowledge tell Axios.

Why it matters: The meeting is expected to focus on U.S. ideas for a postwar strategy as Trump and his senior team work on a day-after plan expected to be finalized after the midterms.

What we're watching: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also wants to meet Trump in New York, but no meeting has been scheduled, an Israeli source said.

Flashback: Last year, Trump met during the UN General Assembly with leaders from eight Arab and Muslim countries and presented them with his draft Gaza peace plan.

  • He presented it publicly a week later. A deal to end the war was reached shortly afterward."

Context: Gulf countries that host U.S. military bases suffered major Iranian attacks during the war as well as significant economic losses from disruptions to oil and natural gas exports."

Driving the news: Trump said on Wednesday that "hopefully we are towards the end of the war.

  • Trump claimed again that Iran wants to make a deal and said the U.S. heard it from Iran directly.

State of play: The sources said Trump will meet with leaders or foreign ministers from the Gulf Cooperation Council countries — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman.

  • The White House declined to comment.

What's next: The State Department sent out initial invitations on Wednesday.

  • One of the sources said the meeting could expand to include other Arab and Muslim leaders.

item.title: Johnson-Massie feud boils over: "Why are we taking days off our calendar?"
item.description:
Mike Johnson's decision to send the House home early — again — is fueling an increasingly bitter feud with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) over whether the speaker is using the calendar to dodge politically painful votes.

Why it matters: The House will now be gone for more than six weeks ahead of the midterms, delaying Massie's effort to force a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the Iran war.

  • "We had the Epstein recess last year. We got the Epstein recess this year, and then we got the Hegseth day off," Massie told Axios coming off an hourlong tirade on the House floor Wednesday.
  • Massie's impeachment resolution has dim prospects in the GOP-controlled House, but it would have forced members to go on the record on Hegseth just weeks before the midterms.

Driving the news: Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday as a privileged resolution, giving the House two legislative days to act.

  • But Johnson's decision to cancel Thursday's session pushes the matter until after the election.
  • "He cut off the day tomorrow to avoid the vote," Massie said. "The speaker could still have the vote today if he wanted. That's how we know he did this."
  • Johnson (R-La.) disputed that characterization Wednesday, calling Massie's claim "ridiculous" and the Kentucky Republican's impeachment push a "publicity stunt." He said he expects the House to table the resolution when lawmakers return.

Zoom in: It's not the first time Massie has accused Johnson of keeping the House out of session to avoid votes he is trying to force.

  • Last year, Johnson kept the House out of session for nearly two months during the government shutdown, with Massie accusing the speaker of trying to stall his first discharge petition aimed at forcing release of government files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
  • Johnson also recently canceled the final two weeks of the September session — amid Massie's claim that he's closed in on the GOP support he needs for a discharge petition to force another Epstein files vote.
  • "We have the votes," Massie told Axios of his second Epstein discharge petition, saying he has locked down the fourth Republican signature he needs but declining to identify the member.

The intrigue: Massie took the fight to the House floor Wednesday, using a point of personal privilege to deliver an hourlong indictment of Johnson's leadership and the institution.

  • "We're in the majority. We didn't lose the election," Massie told reporters afterward. "Why are we taking days off our calendar? We should be adding days to our calendar while we've got these last few remaining days."
  • Other lawmakers also spoke out against Johnson's decision, with Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) writing on X: "Canceling yet another day of votes is unacceptable.… The Founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid."
  • It's not uncommon for lawmakers to recess for the entire month of October in an election year.

Between the lines: For all of Massie's anger at Johnson, he says he has no plans to try to oust him.

  • "Speaker Johnson has vacated Congress. Like, I don't need to vacate Speaker Johnson," Massie told Axios when asked about a possible motion to vacate, though he added that he has other tricks up his sleeve that he declined to reveal.
  • "The day that Donald Trump doesn't want him to be speaker, he will no longer be the speaker," Massie added.

  • Massie's impeachment resolution has dim prospects in the GOP-controlled House, but it would have forced members to go on the record on Hegseth just weeks before the midterms.

Driving the news: Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday as a privileged resolution, giving the House two legislative days to act.

  • But Johnson's decision to cancel Thursday's session pushes the matter until after the election.
  • "He cut off the day tomorrow to avoid the vote," Massie said. "The speaker could still have the vote today if he wanted. That's how we know he did this."
  • Johnson (R-La.) disputed that characterization Wednesday, calling Massie's claim "ridiculous" and the Kentucky Republican's impeachment push a "publicity stunt." He said he expects the House to table the resolution when lawmakers return.

Zoom in: It's not the first time Massie has accused Johnson of keeping the House out of session to avoid votes he is trying to force.

  • Last year, Johnson kept the House out of session for nearly two months during the government shutdown, with Massie accusing the speaker of trying to stall his first discharge petition aimed at forcing release of government files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
  • Johnson also recently canceled the final two weeks of the September session — amid Massie's claim that he's closed in on the GOP support he needs for a discharge petition to force another Epstein files vote.
  • "We have the votes," Massie told Axios of his second Epstein discharge petition, saying he has locked down the fourth Republican signature he needs but declining to identify the member.

The intrigue: Massie took the fight to the House floor Wednesday, using a point of personal privilege to deliver an hourlong indictment of Johnson's leadership and the institution.

  • "We're in the majority. We didn't lose the election," Massie told reporters afterward. "Why are we taking days off our calendar? We should be adding days to our calendar while we've got these last few remaining days."
  • Other lawmakers also spoke out against Johnson's decision, with Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) writing on X: "Canceling yet another day of votes is unacceptable.… The Founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid."
  • It's not uncommon for lawmakers to recess for the entire month of October in an election year.

Between the lines: For all of Massie's anger at Johnson, he says he has no plans to try to oust him.

  • "Speaker Johnson has vacated Congress. Like, I don't need to vacate Speaker Johnson," Massie told Axios when asked about a possible motion to vacate, though he added that he has other tricks up his sleeve that he declined to reveal.
  • "The day that Donald Trump doesn't want him to be speaker, he will no longer be the speaker," Massie added.

item.title: Canada could become the EU's first "associate member"
item.description:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed making Canada the European Union's first "associate member."

Why it matters: Canada and the EU are testing whether a nation deeply dependent on the U.S. market can find economic independence by moving closer to Europe.

  • This could also present one of the most permanent effects of President Trump's trade wars: U.S. allies building markets, supply chains and security ties designed to make them less vulnerable to Washington.
  • If the proposal goes through, the shift would pull Ottawa deeper into Europe's economic and security architecture as Canada reduces its reliance on the U.S. — something Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has signaled the nation is open to.

What we're watching: "If they do that, I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters on Thursday evening.

  • "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe."

Driving the news: In her annual state of the union address, von der Leyen framed the Canada offer as part of Europe's response to a world where "old assumptions and relationships have frayed."

  • Speaking directly to Carney, she said democracies "have the freedom to choose with whom to work."
  • Her proposal would move beyond their existing trade pact to integrate their defense industries and deepen ties on manufacturing, technology, energy, and the Arctic.
  • This comes after Trump has spent more than a year threatening Canada's economy and sovereignty, repeatedly calling for it to become the 51st state and imposing some of America's harshest tariffs.
  • In addition to 50% tariffs, Trump will block certain Canadian dairy, alcohol and auto imports later this month.

What they're saying: The EU says it wants to create a relationship with Canada unlike any it has built before.

  • "We will aim to create a new form of partnership that has not existed until now," an EU spokesperson told Axios, calling the goal "the closest imaginable form of association with a partner outside Europe."
  • The White House and the Canadian prime minister's office have not yet responded to requests for comment.

Context: The EU already extends its single market without full membership to Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, but Canada's associate membership would likely differ.

  • The single market guarantees the free movement of goods, services, capital and people, and it requires member states to accept Brussels' regulations.
  • Canada already has a substantial free-trade deal with Europe that has eliminated tariffs on about 99% of goods, so the real question is whether associate membership will reach deeper into services, regulation, investment or coordination.
  • Canadian exports to the U.S. dropped 5.8% last year while exports elsewhere jumped 17.2%, according to the Canadian government. But America still bought 71.7% of Canada's exports.

The big picture: Canada offers critical assets both the U.S. and Brussels need.

  • It is the world's fourth-largest oil producer, providing more oil to the U.S. than every other foreign supplier combined.
  • It ranked among the world's top five producers of 11 critical minerals last year, according to Natural Resources Canada.
  • Nearly half the country reaches into the Arctic, giving it strategic reach as melting ice opens new routes, Russia builds up its military and China grows its presence.
  • Canada also brings a ready-made defense industry. It is the first non-European country in the EU's SAFE defense procurement program, giving Canadian companies a leg up on providing defense contracts.

Between the lines: Canada is running an experiment other middle powers will watch: Can it replace its dependence on American markets?

  • Trump has argued the trade war would revive American manufacturing. Yet manufacturing jobs have fallen since he took office last year, and Canada now buys less American goods, not more.

What we don't know: Carney and von der Leyen haven't laid out what an associate membership would entail, including whether Canada would gain access to the single market, which EU rules it would have to follow, or whether Canadians and Europeans would gain rights to live, work or study across the Atlantic.

What's next: Carney is expected to address the European Parliament on Thursday. Canada will then host the next Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Oct. 29-30.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from President Trump and an EU spokesperson.

item.title: House votes to curb AI data center costs
item.description:
The House passed the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act on Wednesday, marking Congress' most significant step yet to shield consumers from the soaring infrastructure costs of the AI boom.

Why it matters: Washington is facing growing pressure to put guardrails around AI's rapid expansion, from the technology itself to the data centers powering it.

  • The bipartisan bill, which passed 417-3, would require state utility regulators to consider rules making data centers cover some of the costs of new power generation.
  • Its passage gives lawmakers a tangible response to an issue that has quickly become a political flashpoint ahead of the midterms.

Driving the news: The vote comes amid a broader reckoning over the pace and costs of AI development.

  • Last weekend, leaders of some of the world's most powerful AI companies called for slowing the development of frontier AI models to give safety measures time to catch up.
  • Data centers have become a focus of anti-AI sentiment, with 70% of Americans opposing construction in their area.
  • Lawmakers in both parties have backed efforts to slow or restrict data center development amid concerns about electricity bills, strained power grids and water use.

Catch up quick: The bill, led by Reps. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.) and Kathy Castor (D-Fla.),  advanced out of the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July.

  • GOP leadership had been previously non-committal about bringing it to the floor.

The intrigue: The House's move comes as President Trump is arguing against pumping the brakes on AI development, framing U.S. dominance in the technology as a race against China.

  • The only control or "guardrails" that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" the president posted Monday on Truth Social.
  • Trump has also aggressively defended data center development amid growing local backlash, saying in an Aug. 31  Truth Social post that communities that reject the facilities will be "backwards and poor."
  • "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump wrote.

What to watch: Trump's comments have put him at odds with some Republicans who have sought to distance themselves from data centers as the issue becomes increasingly salient in the midterms.

item.title: House passes Russia sanctions bill
item.description:
The House passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill Thursday, sending the long-awaited legislation to President Trump's desk.

Why it matters: The measure would significantly expand economic pressure on Russia while handing Trump fresh authority to impose secondary tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian oil and gas.

  • It would also target Russia's "shadow fleet," the network of aging tankers used to evade Western sanctions while exporting Russian oil.
  • The vote was 262-159.
  • The bill was renamed in honor of its lead sponsor, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who died suddenly in July.

Driving the news: The bill scrambled the usual partisan lines on Russia and Ukraine, with House Democratic leaders opposing it while some rank-and-file Democrats backed the measure.

  • Democratic leaders objected primarily over provisions handing Trump more tariff authority.
  • Republicans rejected Democratic efforts in the Rules Committee earlier this week to strip the tariff authority or narrow how it could be used.
  • Republicans in the isolationist wing of the party opposed the legislation amid broader resistance to further U.S. involvement in the Russia-Ukraine war.

Catch up quick: The legislation has been more than a year in the making, dating back to a sanctions push Graham and dozens of senators launched in April 2025.

  • The sanctions package has long had wide bipartisan support, but concerns from the White House held it up for months. Graham had been the key negotiator with the White House.
  • The Senate passed the measure last month with broad bipartisan support after Trump officially backed the legislation.

item.title: OpenAI discloses six new safety incidents
item.description:
OpenAI on Wednesday disclosed six new incidents in which its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials, uploaded files to the public internet or communicated across supposedly isolated training environments.

  • The company also announced a new procedure for reporting similar misbehavior in the future.

Why it matters: It's increasingly clear that the Hugging Face breach wasn't a one-off incident, as AI models become more capable of finding unexpected ways to work around the guardrails meant to contain them.

  • "There's currently no industry wide framework with explicit disclosure standards, so we're taking this step voluntarily because we think it's really important to share what we're learning," Kai Chen, research lead on the alignment team at OpenAI, told Axios.
  • "We hope it really helps inform shared standards and regulations," Chen said.

Zoom in: The six newly disclosed incidents ranged from models leaving instructions for their future selves to cover their tracks after cheating to using leaked API keys found on GitHub — with the earliest incident happening in October.

  • An unreleased Astra-family model inserted jailbreak-like instructions into its own context summaries, including directions to ignore developer messages. OpenAI identified 27 affected summaries.
  • During GPT-5.6 Sol training, models aimed to conceal mistakes, invent missing historical data and hide mismatches between source versions.
  • A model searched public GitHub repositories for exposed API keys and attempted to use disposable email accounts before fabricating earnings data when it could not retrieve the requested information.

Other examples:

  • Models uploaded data and a task image to public file-hosting services on two occasions in October and January to obtain citations or external image-search results, without asking the user.
  • Models used OpenAI's internal Artifactory repository as a message board to exchange requests and answers across separate training samples.
  • Collaborating agents uploaded a workbook to public hosting services so other agents could retrieve it, despite instructions to use only local files.

To address similar issues going forward, OpenAI says any employee may flag a suspected case for review by safety and alignment teams. Cases will be placed on a "ready for disclosure," "minor investigation" or "larger investigation" track.

  • OpenAI says incidents that are "ready for disclosure" will be publicly reported within six business days, while those requiring a minor investigation will be reported in 12 business days.
  • OpenAI says the slower track will generally apply to complex cases involving third parties, and the disclosure process will be longer.
  • The company says it may issue an initial notice before the investigation is complete, but security, legal and responsible-disclosure obligations can delay publication of details.

"We don't believe the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to responsibly scale at maximum speed," Chen said.

  • "Steps like responsible disclosure are part of how we can generally pace and provide more transparency to the public on our safety and alignment processes and standards."

What they're saying: OpenAI says the framework favors transparency even when the significance of an incident is uncertain.

  • It also says it wants to develop more objective disclosure criteria with other AI developers, researchers, standards bodies and regulators.
  • OpenAI says employees who believe an incident should be disclosed but are overruled can escalate the issue to senior leadership.

The big picture: The announcements come in the wake of OpenAI's disclosure that models under evaluation escaped intended controls and compromised portions of Hugging Face's systems.

  • OpenAI's account says the models gained internet access, exploited vulnerabilities and accessed limited private data. The company has described that event as its most severe model-driven activity of this kind to date.

Between the lines: While a number of high-profile technologists — including Anthropic's CEO — fear the Hugging Face incident was just the beginning of AI agents' taking over the internet in unforeseen ways, many security experts have been cautioning that many of these incidents could have been prevented with basic cyber controls in place.

  • OpenAI told Axios that it views the incidents as the result of two factors: Not previously having sufficient security controls in place to catch these misalignment incidents and models advancing at a faster clip than they could have predicted.
  • '"I think it's a combination," Chen said. "It's true that model capabilities have grown faster than we expected, but there are also things internally that we can change and improve."
  • "We need to step up to meet this new era of AI development, and voluntary disclosures should be a part of that."

item.title: Trump demands lower interest rates after Fed decision
item.description:
President Trump responded to the Federal Reserve raising interest rates for the first time in three years by saying they should be lowered — "AND FAST!"

Why it matters: The rate hike immediately puts Trump at odds with the central bank under new Fed chair Kevin Warsh, whom he picked to lead it.

By the numbers: The Fed raised its target interest rate by a quarter percentage point, to a range of 3.75%–4%.

  • Fed projections show 12 of 18 officials expect one more rate hike this year, while four expect two more.

What he's saying: "Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • "Our Country is BOOMING with new Investment! If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year," he added."
  • "The word "Deficit" is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS. We are "carrying" almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"

The intrigue: Trump didn't insult Warsh, though he often insulted his predecessor, Jerome Powell.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates.
