item.title: U.S. diplomats meet with Houthis as Red Sea crisis intensifies
item.description:
American diplomats met over the weekend with Houthi representatives at the U.S. embassy in Oman and discussed tensions in the Red Sea, a regional source familiar with the issue confirmed.

Why it matters: The meeting in Muscat, which was organized with the help of the Omani government, focused on maintaining a ceasefire between the U.S. and Houthis and guaranteeing that the Bab al-Mandeb Strait stays open, the source said.

  • The U.S. is in a delicate position, wanting to keep a vital shipping lane open without getting drawn into Saudi Arabia's battle in Yemen against the Iran-backed Houthis. Washington has so far rejected Saudi requests to get involved militarily.

Driving the news: The source said the U.S. was represented in the meeting by diplomats from the embassy, but the ambassador did not attend.

  • The person added that Houthi representatives made clear during the meeting that they wanted the May 2025 ceasefire with the U.S. to continue.
  • The source also said that Houthi representatives stressed their attacks were aimed only at Saudi ships as part of the renewed fighting between the two sides. They committed to allow freedom of navigation for all other ships through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
  • Reuters first reported on the meeting.

What they're saying: "The United States' core interests in the Middle East include ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the region, as well as preventing the export of terrorism. The Trump Administration has clearly demonstrated its commitment to defending these interests against aggression from Iran and its proxies," a State Department spokesperson said in a statement.

  • "We have no comment on this specific reported meeting," the statement continued. "However, we remain in regular communication with our regional allies and partners regarding Yemen and are focused on our shared counterterrorism goals against the Houthis and other terrorist groups that sow chaos throughout the region."

On Monday, a day after the meeting, Vice President Vance told reporters that the U.S. is negotiating with the Houthis.

  • "We've also been engaged in direct conversations with the Houthis themselves, so we actually feel like we are on top of the situation," he said.

Between the lines: Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke on Tuesday with Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi about efforts to deescalate in the region, the State Department said.

  • The call came after weeks of tensions between the U.S. and Oman. President Trump threatened to bomb Oman because of talks it had held with Iran about the Strait of Hormuz.

State of play: The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been escalating in recent days, with the Houthis launching a drone attack toward the holy city of Mecca and firing missiles at other cities in the kingdom.

  • The Houthis are still in control of the coastal area and several islands in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
  • The Saudis have increased their airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. But the forces they're backing in Yemen have so far been unable to launch an effective ground counteroffensive.
item.content:encoded:
American diplomats met over the weekend with Houthi representatives at the U.S. embassy in Oman and discussed tensions in the Red Sea, a regional source familiar with the issue confirmed.

Why it matters: The meeting in Muscat, which was organized with the help of the Omani government, focused on maintaining a ceasefire between the U.S. and Houthis and guaranteeing that the Bab al-Mandeb Strait stays open, the source said.

  • The U.S. is in a delicate position, wanting to keep a vital shipping lane open without getting drawn into Saudi Arabia's battle in Yemen against the Iran-backed Houthis. Washington has so far rejected Saudi requests to get involved militarily.

Driving the news: The source said the U.S. was represented in the meeting by diplomats from the embassy, but the ambassador did not attend.

  • The person added that Houthi representatives made clear during the meeting that they wanted the May 2025 ceasefire with the U.S. to continue.
  • The source also said that Houthi representatives stressed their attacks were aimed only at Saudi ships as part of the renewed fighting between the two sides. They committed to allow freedom of navigation for all other ships through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
  • Reuters first reported on the meeting.

What they're saying: "The United States' core interests in the Middle East include ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the region, as well as preventing the export of terrorism. The Trump Administration has clearly demonstrated its commitment to defending these interests against aggression from Iran and its proxies," a State Department spokesperson said in a statement.

  • "We have no comment on this specific reported meeting," the statement continued. "However, we remain in regular communication with our regional allies and partners regarding Yemen and are focused on our shared counterterrorism goals against the Houthis and other terrorist groups that sow chaos throughout the region."

On Monday, a day after the meeting, Vice President Vance told reporters that the U.S. is negotiating with the Houthis.

  • "We've also been engaged in direct conversations with the Houthis themselves, so we actually feel like we are on top of the situation," he said.

Between the lines: Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke on Tuesday with Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi about efforts to deescalate in the region, the State Department said.

  • The call came after weeks of tensions between the U.S. and Oman. President Trump threatened to bomb Oman because of talks it had held with Iran about the Strait of Hormuz.

State of play: The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been escalating in recent days, with the Houthis launching a drone attack toward the holy city of Mecca and firing missiles at other cities in the kingdom.

  • The Houthis are still in control of the coastal area and several islands in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
  • The Saudis have increased their airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. But the forces they're backing in Yemen have so far been unable to launch an effective ground counteroffensive.

item.title: Scoop: U.S. open to discuss AI "shared risks" with China, Bessent says
item.description:
The U.S. is open to discussing shared risks with China in upcoming AI talks this weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios.

Why it matters: The Trump administration has flatly rejected calls from industry to pace or slow down the development of AI, citing a fierce race against China.

  • Bessent's scheduled meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng could provide an opening for talks on U.S.-China AI safety cooperation.

"The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems. We expect our discussions to cover both open and closed weight models," Bessent said in a statement to Axios.

  • "Bessent and [United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer] are the point guys on China. So it makes sense the secretary is in this position," a senior administration official said.

Driving the news: There will be multi-hour meetings in New York City, focused on AI, trade, rare earths, and other economic issues, building on previous discussions held in cities around the world, sources familiar said.

  • The agenda will remain flexible to allow for substantive discussion across the range of relevant issues, sources added.
  • Possible working-level meetings will continue into Monday, sources said.

Catch up quick: Bessent has played a key role in the Trump administration's AI agenda.

  • He was among the few cabinet members who flanked President Trump during a G7 press conference in June, where top AI CEOs and the administration discussed a U.S.-led effort to coordinate global AI standards.
  • Bessent also helped cool Anthropic's relations with the administration following a fallout with the Pentagon and is viewed as a reasonable actor who is trusted by the private sector and critical infrastructure operators, sources familiar have previously told Axios.
  • Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick led high-profile AI discussions during the G20 summit in North Carolina earlier this month, while Bessent is taking the lead on talks with China.

The big picture: Bessent's meetings in New York come days before Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's summit in Washington on Sept. 24.

  • AI CEOs have been calling for U.S.-China coordination on safety standards.
  • "All parties should jointly promote the open and inclusive development of AI for good and for all," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said this week, while pushing back on U.S. AI companies' calls to slow down and warning against "fear-mongering."

The bottom line: While a major breakthrough in U.S.-China safety cooperation remains a tall order, Bessent's involvement signals room for engagement on AI between the competing countries.

item.title: AI environmental concerns build as lawmakers grapple with tech panic
item.description:
Data: The AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about the environmental impacts of AI, up more than ten percentage points from last year, per polling results out Wednesday.

The big picture: It's just one area where Americans' AI concerns are building across the spectrum — highlighting one of the few issues lawmakers are crossing the aisle to confront amid ballooning panic set off by rogue models, industry warnings and public backlash.

  • But it's unclear what, if any, role the AI backlash will play in the upcoming midterm elections, with voters split on who is better suited to handle the issue. Some Democratic lawmakers are reportedly hesitant to spend too much time discussing it on the campaign trail.
  • President Trump has emerged as a top cheerleader for AI and the data centers needed to power the tech, with his administration moving to reshape environmental and permitting regulations for AI infrastructure.

Driving the news: But that comes as 53% of Americans are extremely or very concerned about the environmental impacts of AI, according to a poll of 3,424 from The AP-NORC Center and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) conducted July 6 to 24.

  • Democrats are more likely than Republicans to be extremely or very concerned at 65%, but 42% of Republicans shared that sentiment — a larger share than those who are somewhat concerned (26%) or not concerned at all (31%).
  • Democrats are also more likely to say AI will be hurtful to society as a whole, per the polling, but half of Republicans are similarly pessimistic.
  • Anxiety about data centers' impact on electricity prices, power outages or water supply is also wide-ranging, with roughly eight in 10 adults reporting being at least somewhat concerned about each.

Zoom out: Separate polling out today found that a significant slice of Americans also share a far more existential concern: that AI could one day destroy humanity.

  • More than six in 10 Americans say there's at least a moderate risk that happens, per The POLITICO Poll. Majorities across the aisle hold that view.
  • A plurality also say AI developers should hit pause.

Friction point: Three Anthropic researchers set off a firestorm of concern last week when they went public with warnings that AI could destroy humans this decade.

  • Despite leaders' calls for a slowdown in the race, Trump remains in a full-steam-ahead headspace, arguing the "only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT."
  • Meanwhile, on Capitol Hill, a flurry of initiatives are grappling with the AI boom, from a bipartisan caucus on AI small businesses to legislation establishing a federal program to monitor systems.
  • More than 100 House Democrats signed onto a letter urging House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to cancel the upcoming recess to vote on AI safeguards — but he signaled today that's not happening.

What they're saying: Reid Hoffman, LinkedIn co-founder and a major Democratic donor, contended in a Wednesday essay that neither the extreme accelerationist and decelerationist camps have the ideal approach. But the next three years, he says, will set the course for AI's societal impact.

  • He wrote, "the next 36 months will be determinative; we need an engaged public and leaders who understand and can deliver on the dual American mandate of economic prosperity and global AI leadership. That is the task in front of us now."

Go deeper: An aging Congress attempts to regulate AI without using it

item.title: Exclusive: Warren backs pause on advanced AI
item.description:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is the latest prominent Democrat to back a pause on advanced artificial intelligence, her office told Axios exclusively.

Why it matters: The idea of slowing down AI development — once considered a non-starter in a fierce race to beat China — is gaining momentum.

Driving the news: Warren on Wednesday will call for a pause on advanced AI development but will stop short of calling for a ban on superintelligence, breaking with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

  • "We should immediately press pause on the development of advanced AI while lawmakers and regulators put systems in place to keep people safe," Warren will say ahead of a roundtable hosted by Sanders on Wednesday.
  • "Congress must urgently pass legislation to put stronger guardrails in place before we have a cyberattack, economic crisis, or national security disaster facilitated by AI."
  • Sanders' proposal calls for a pause and a ban on superintelligence, and threatens up to 20 years in prison for violations, which its authors note is similar to the penalties for illegally developing nuclear weapons.

Between the lines: The progressive movement — like every other political faction — does not have a unified position when it comes to the nitty-gritty of AI regulation.

  • Warren and Sanders have also released AI tax plans with varying approaches.
  • Warren has proposed taxing AI companies, while Sanders wants the government to take equity stakes in them.

Catch up quick: Frontier lab CEOs have coalesced around a message of pacing or slowing frontier AI development and seeking international collaboration.

  • Warren said the industry's push to "pace the frontier" is "insufficient," arguing that elected officials, not AI CEOs, should decide the technology's future. Suggestions to weaken antitrust protections to confront AI risks are "transparently self-serving," she said.
  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for an exemption in antitrust law to help coordinate AI pacing.
  • Former antitrust government officials say that would not be necessary because the law does not prevent AI companies from coordinating to prevent harm and sharing legitimate cybersecurity information.

The big picture: More Democrats with national profiles are weighing in on the idea of a pause as the Trump administration flatly rejects it.

  • Kamala Harris this week endorsed slowing down and called on President Trump to pursue a treaty with China.
  • Barack Obama also backed the idea of slowing down as a good first step.

The bottom line: More Democrats are calling to slow AI development, but there's little agreement on what government should do about it.

item.title: Exclusive: Kristen Silverberg named next president and CEO of Business Roundtable
item.description:
Kristen Silverberg, a widely respected policy expert and former ambassador, was named the new president and CEO of Business Roundtable, the top policy voice of America's leading CEOs.

  • Silverberg, now BRT's president and chief operating officer, will succeed Josh Bolten, a former White House chief of staff who has led the organization for the past decade, when he steps down on Jan. 31.

Why it matters: Business Roundtable is one of Washington's most influential associations. The 200+ members are CEOs of the biggest U.S.-based companies, most with global reach.

  • The CEOs use BRT to amplify what they consider the most important messages business leaders can deliver to government.

Silverberg — who worked with Bolten in the White House and is a former U.S. ambassador to the European Union from 2008 to 2009 — said in a statement that a key mission of BRT, American companies and their CEOs is championing and delivering growth and jobs.

  • "The American economy is undergoing a profound transformation," she said. "Leaders in government and business have an extraordinary opportunity and a responsibility to strengthen American growth and competitiveness while expanding opportunity for workers and communities."
  • "Business Roundtable has a critical role to play in advancing policies that make America the best place in the world to build, grow and invest in a business."

The backstory: Silverberg, 55, was an assistant secretary of State under President George W. Bush and was a law clerk to Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas and Judge David Sentelle of the U.S. Court of Appeals. 

  • She's a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Texas School of Law.

What they're saying: BRT chair Chuck Robbins, chair and CEO of Cisco Systems, called Silverberg a "proven and strategic leader, with the deep trust and respect of Business Roundtable's Board and members."

  • "Kristen has been instrumental in positioning the organization and its leaders as effective advocates for policies that help American businesses grow and innovate while expanding opportunity for workers and communities across the country."

Bolten told me in an interview: "Kristen Silverberg is one of the finest policy professionals in America today. Over the last several years, she earned broad respect among Business Roundtable members and the enthusiastic support of BRT's board.

  • "I could not be happier that they have selected Kristen to lead BRT through the challenging years ahead."

What's next: Bolten, already a member of several major boards, plans a "portfolio" approach for his next phase.

  • 🏟️ On his bucket list: visiting all 30 Major League Baseball ballparks with his son.

item.title: An aging Congress attempts to regulate AI without using it
item.description:
Members of Congress and governors are under increasing pressure to regulate AI, but more than two dozen of them who spoke with Axios said they don't use the technology or have rarely done so.

Why it matters: That striking admission — particularly among older, influential lawmakers — comes amid calls for an AI slowdown and warnings within the industry that it could end humanity if left unchecked.

  • Critics argue that it's impossible for politicians to grasp how rapidly the technology is changing — and the threats or scientific breakthroughs it might unleash — if they don't use it or even dismiss it.

One House Democrat called it "f*cking absurd," arguing, "Anyone who's overseeing this has to be someone who's a regular user."

  • "That's a real problem," said Rob Flaherty, a 35-year-old Democratic digital strategist who co-founded a group to push his party to move faster in confronting AI. "Understanding what it can do is essential to figuring out what we ought to do about it."
  • "As we begin to legislate on issues related to AI, it helps to have experience using it," said Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.), who's 47.

Zoom in: Several lawmakers, including those steeped in seniority and in charge of key committees, told Axios they simply haven't tried AI.

  • "Heavens no," said Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), 75, chair of the Armed Services Committee, when asked if he uses AI.
  • "Personally? I don't think I've ever used it," said Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), 74, the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
  • "No," Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai'i), 78, said when asked if she uses AI, but that "doesn't mean I won't." She added, "I don't think we in Congress have gotten quite our handle on what we should do and how much AI we should be regulating."

"I do not personally use it," said Sen. James Risch (R-Idaho), 83, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair.

  • On a personal level, "no," said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), 83. The House Appropriations Committee ranking member added that she needs a "primer on AI, and now with the scare that we have out there, it's much more important to be engaged."
  • A GOP senator, speaking anonymously to offer candid remarks about their colleagues, told Axios that the number who use AI is "not very high."
  • That's helped lead to a knee-jerk negative reaction toward AI among several lawmakers, the senator added, as polls show growing numbers of voters turning against it.

Some elected officials said they don't utilize AI much personally, though some on their teams employ the technology.

  • Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), who's 48, said he uses AI "on the Google, when you can get a little bit of that search summarized for you. But otherwise no. I do not use it in research. We do not use it in our writing."
  • He said that he supports robust regulation and though some in his state government use AI, final decisions must be made by humans.

Other politicians were unsure if they've ever used AI — or said they've only done so by accident.

  • "I don't think I do," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), 70, when asked if he utilizes it. "If I Google something, it kicks off an AI thing, but that's about as far as I go."
  • "I don't know. I can't remember," said Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), 88.
  • Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), 73, said she doesn't seek out AI on her own, but that "it pops up on my phone occasionally."
  • "Not intentionally," said Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), 68. "The only AI use that I'm kind of familiar with is an AI tool attempting to summarize email chains, and they often get it wrong."

What they're saying: Some lawmakers such as Kaine argued that they don't need to use AI to write legislation about it. He said he has read a lot about it and trusts his judgment more than AI.

  • After we spoke with him, Pallone shared a statement through a spokesperson that said: "You don't need to do drugs like heroin to know they should be regulated. Members of Congress don't need to spend their time talking to AI chatbots all day to know we need to rein in this dangerous technology."

Friction point: But some members of Congress were irked or surprised that colleagues don't use a technology they're seeking to regulate.

  • "Are you serious?" Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), 74, said in response to our question. "I use it for everything! I can't believe there's a senator that doesn't use AI."

Yes, but: There are members of Congress who are frequent AI users, including some in Hickenlooper's age range.

  • Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), 79, the ranking member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, told Axios he uses AI "every day."
  • Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), 76, went back to school to get a master's degree in machine learning and said he prefers Claude.

Catch up quick: Some of the most powerful elected officials in the country have told other media outlets in the recent past that they don't use AI.

  • In late 2025, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), 54, said in an interview that he didn't think he'd ever used AI.
  • About the same time, Karoline Leavitt, then press secretary to President Trump, 80, said that she didn't think Trump personally uses AI, though his social media account regularly posts AI-made content.

  • "No," Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai'i), 78, said when asked if she uses AI, but that "doesn't mean I won't." She added, "I don't think we in Congress have gotten quite our handle on what we should do and how much AI we should be regulating."

"I do not personally use it," said Sen. James Risch (R-Idaho), 83, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair.

  • On a personal level, "no," said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), 83. The House Appropriations Committee ranking member added that she needs a "primer on AI, and now with the scare that we have out there, it's much more important to be engaged."
  • A GOP senator, speaking anonymously to offer candid remarks about their colleagues, told Axios that the number who use AI is "not very high."
  • That's helped lead to a knee-jerk negative reaction toward AI among several lawmakers, the senator added, as polls show growing numbers of voters turning against it.

Some elected officials said they don't utilize AI much personally, though some on their teams employ the technology.

  • Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), who's 48, said he uses AI "on the Google, when you can get a little bit of that search summarized for you. But otherwise no. I do not use it in research. We do not use it in our writing."
  • He said that he supports robust regulation and though some in his state government use AI, final decisions must be made by humans.

Other politicians were unsure if they've ever used AI — or said they've only done so by accident.

  • "I don't think I do," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), 70, when asked if he utilizes it. "If I Google something, it kicks off an AI thing, but that's about as far as I go."
  • "I don't know. I can't remember," said Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), 88.
  • Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), 73, said she doesn't seek out AI on her own, but that "it pops up on my phone occasionally."
  • "Not intentionally," said Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), 68. "The only AI use that I'm kind of familiar with is an AI tool attempting to summarize email chains, and they often get it wrong."

What they're saying: Some lawmakers such as Kaine argued that they don't need to use AI to write legislation about it. He said he has read a lot about it and trusts his judgment more than AI.

  • After we spoke with him, Pallone shared a statement through a spokesperson that said: "You don't need to do drugs like heroin to know they should be regulated. Members of Congress don't need to spend their time talking to AI chatbots all day to know we need to rein in this dangerous technology."

Friction point: But some members of Congress were irked or surprised that colleagues don't use a technology they're seeking to regulate.

  • "Are you serious?" Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), 74, said in response to our question. "I use it for everything! I can't believe there's a senator that doesn't use AI."

Yes, but: There are members of Congress who are frequent AI users, including some in Hickenlooper's age range.

  • Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), 79, the ranking member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, told Axios he uses AI "every day."
  • Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), 76, went back to school to get a master's degree in machine learning and said he prefers Claude.

Catch up quick: Some of the most powerful elected officials in the country have told other media outlets in the recent past that they don't use AI.

  • In late 2025, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), 54, said in an interview that he didn't think he'd ever used AI.
  • About the same time, Karoline Leavitt, then press secretary to President Trump, 80, said that she didn't think Trump personally uses AI, though his social media account regularly posts AI-made content.

item.title: Trump escalates war on federal data
item.description:
The nerdy, traditionally apolitical world of federal data is increasingly getting swept up in the Trump administration's push to control every level of government.

  • Across the federal government, agencies are changing how they collect and publicize information. More and more, politics and ideology are part of the equation.

Why it matters: Reliable, unbiased data informs nearly everything the federal government does — from distributing benefits and enforcing workplace discrimination laws to responding to public health threats.

Driving the news: The administration's moves in recent weeks span an array of agencies and types of data.

🩺 Measles. Reuters reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked the CDC director to remove a reference to two deaths in Pennsylvania from its online tally of measles cases.

  • The move came after the CDC had already accepted Pennsylvania officials' explanation that the deaths were linked to measles.
  • Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro had spent days sparring on social media, each accusing the other of politicizing the deaths. Kennedy is a longtime vaccine skeptic.

🏡 Census Bureau. Last month, the Commerce Department did away with language barring political interference that had been part of the department's scientific integrity policy, NPR reported. The department oversees the Census Bureau and several other agencies.

  • The move came after the bureau issued an unauthored report — promptly touted by President Trump — that found that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election.
  • The team behind the report, however, included officials with ties to the Trump-linked America First Institute.

⚠️ Anti-discrimination. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is planning to stop collecting data that's helped the agency investigate claims of workplace discrimination, The Guardian reported.

  • For 60 years, the agency has examined the demographic makeup of company workforces to enforce anti-discrimination laws.
  • The EEOC is now planning to do away with the so-called EEO-1 reports, which require companies to provide data on their workforces broken down by race, ethnicity, sex and job title.
  • The move comes amid a broader Trump administration crackdown on DEI — diversity, equity and inclusion — initiatives.
  • At a July hearing, Andrea Lucas, an EEOC commissioner appointed by Trump, said the data collection was burdensome for employers and encouraged discrimination against white workers, per the Guardian.

What they're saying: "The level of politicization in this administration is beyond anything I've seen," says Denice Ross, former U.S. chief data scientist and currently director of the Data Policy Institute at the Federation of American Scientists. "I've been doing this work for 25 years."

Zoom out: Fears about the handling of data that doesn't comport with Trump's worldview have been around for years.

  • Last year, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics hours after the agency released disappointing jobs numbers. "Today's Jobs Numbers were RIGGED in order to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad," Trump wrote.
  • The Department of Homeland Security has stopped regularly publishing comprehensive immigration enforcement statistics, including data that allowed outsiders to assess the administration's deportation efforts. The official who oversaw DHS's independent statistics office resigned in July, The Atlantic reported.
  • According to a tracker run by former federal government data scientists, 38 datasets have been eliminated since Trump returned to office. Hundreds of other datasets have been altered or disrupted.

The other side: "The Trump administration is committed to providing the American people with timely, accurate, and relevant data that's helpful to inform meaningful research, discourse, and decision-making," White House spokesman Kush Desai said.

  • "Ensuring public health and other critical data actually reflect reality while refusing to waste taxpayer resources on ideological pet projects are all important parts of that mission."

The bottom line: "We really take data for granted," Ross said. "It's invisible infrastructure, like a bridge or cell service. We don't notice until it's gone."

item.title: Household income hits record, but lower earners lose ground
item.description:
Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, 1968 to 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplements; Note: Census identifies breaks in the series in 2013 and 2017 due to methodological changes; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios

U.S. household income hit a record in 2025, but the lowest earners barely shared in the gains, new Census data show.

Why it matters: On paper, Americans look richer than ever. But broader measures of financial security show millions still getting squeezed by medical costs, uneven income gains and a thinning public safety net.

  • The 2025 Census report largely captures the economy before the major safety-net reductions in President Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill" took hold.
  • That makes this year's record income and near-record-low official poverty numbers an important benchmark for measuring what happens next.

By the numbers: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, the highest inflation-adjusted level since Census records began in 1967.

  • Median post-tax household income climbed 3.1% to $76,060.
  • The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year, dropping slightly to 10.2%, or about 34.5 million people.
  • Child poverty fell to a record-low 13.4%, while poverty among Hispanics dropped to an unprecedented 13.9%.

State of play: The economy delivered historic topline numbers without spreading the gains evenly.

  • Income among the wealthiest 10% of Americans rose 1.7%, while income among the bottom 10% showed no significant change — indicating that the low-income households largely missed out on the gains.
  • Households at the 90th percentile earned about $261,300, more than 13 times the roughly $20,010 earned at the 10th percentile.
  • The top fifth of households captured 52.4% of all household income. The bottom fifth reported earning just 3%.

Zoom in: Latinos offer one of the clearest examples of the split-screen economy in 2025.

  • Hispanic poverty fell to its lowest level since Census began tracking it in 1973. But the median household income among Hispanics, $73,260, showed no significant change from 2024.
  • Meanwhile, 21.8% of Hispanic adults ages 19 to 64 were uninsured in 2025, down a bit from the previous year — but still the highest uninsured rate among the major racial and ethnic groups shown by Census

Yes, but: Big racial income gaps remain even as some groups posted gains.

  • Asian American households had the highest median income at $126,300 in 2025, compared with $91,930 for white households and $59,980 for Black American households.
  • Black Americans' household income rose 4.8% from 2024 and whites' household income rose 3%, while Asian Americans' household income showed no significant change.

Zoom out: A broader measure of hardship paints a less rosy picture.

  • The Supplemental Poverty Measure, which factors in taxes, government benefits, housing, work and medical expenses, held statistically steady at 13.1% — nearly 3 percentage points above the government's official poverty rate.
  • Medical expenses put an estimated 7.7 million more people below the supplemental poverty line in 2025, the Census Bureau said.

Between the lines: Health insurance coverage held steady overall in 2025. The uninsured rate remained statistically unchanged at 7.9%, or 26.7 million people.

  • Medicaid coverage fell 0.5 percentage points nationally, from 17.6% to 17.1% of the population — representing about 1.4 million fewer people with Medicaid coverage in 2025 than in the previous year
  • Among adults ages 19 to 64, 17.3% had public health coverage — including Medicaid, Medicare and VA/CHAMPVA coverage — down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.
  • Census says the decline was driven by a 0.6-point drop in Medicaid coverage among working-age adults.

What we're watching: The 2025 numbers may represent the last snapshot before major federal safety-net cuts begin showing up in the Census data, Robert Greenstein, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution, tells Axios.

item.title: Tech giants launch flexible-power coalition for data centers
item.description:
A new coalition launched Wednesday is seeking a triple win for a data center industry that lately has struggled to notch any wins at all.

The big picture: Tech giants Google and Nvidia are partnering with startup Emerald AI to back data centers that can flex their power demand — a strategy they say could curb electricity prices, mollify angry neighbors and grow the economy with more AI infrastructure.

  • The launch comes amid mounting backlash to data centers centered on their resource impacts and power prices, and new polling shows the public-opinion challenge is getting steeper.

What they're saying: "It's really a win-win-win solution," said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at Nvidia, in a call with reporters Monday ahead of the official launch of the coalition, called the AI Energy Management Alliance.

State of play: The coalition brings together 20 companies and organizations spanning the AI and energy sectors, including Anthropic, utilities National Grid and AES, and power producers Constellation, NRG and RWE.

  • The group is technically a relaunch. An earlier iteration, the Advanced Energy Management Alliance, was founded in 2014 to advocate for demand-response companies but had become largely inactive, Emerald AI CEO Varun Sivaram said on Monday's call.
  • The revamped group is narrowly focused on making AI data centers more flexible power users — and convincing regulators and utilities to reward them for it.

Friction point: A whopping 84% of Americans say they're concerned about data centers' impact on local electricity prices, according to new AP-NORC/University of Chicago Energy Policy Institute polling released Wednesday.

  • More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about AI's environmental impacts, up from 41% a year ago.
  • In a rare point of bipartisan agreement, roughly equal shares of Democrats and Republicans — 79% and 76%, respectively — support requiring data center developers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to support them.

How it works: Data centers have traditionally been treated as giant, round-the-clock power users. The coalition wants to change the rules so facilities that can reliably cut their grid demand when electricity supplies are tight can get connected faster and potentially avoid some costly grid upgrades.

  • The flexibility could come from shifting or pausing AI computing jobs, tapping batteries or nearby power generation, coalition leaders said.
  • Google has committed 1 gigawatt of power demand it can reduce when needed through utility agreements nationwide, said Tyler Norris, Google's head of advanced energy market innovation.
  • The group plans to push the approach with federal and state regulators, regional grid operators and utilities.

Yes, but: The bargain depends on data centers actually delivering the flexibility they promise. Sivaram said facilities should qualify for faster or larger connections only if their ability to cut demand is "verifiable and enforceable."

Reality check: Convincing communities that this complicated solution can actually address their concerns will be a tall order.

  • "Power-flexible data centers are a wonky topic," Sivaram told Axios.
  • His pitch: Data centers could cut their electricity use when the grid is stressed, helping avoid costly infrastructure while bringing in revenue that can support other electricity users.
  • The goal, Sivaram said, is to turn data centers into "good grid citizens" that communities see as assets rather than burdens.

What we're watching: Whether regulators actually create the fast lane the coalition wants.

  • Federal regulators in June directed regional grid operators to examine new options for connecting large, flexible power users, providing an opening for the approach AEMA is advocating.

Editor's note: Amy Harder is a fellow at the University of Chicago's Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth, but was not involved in the polling and received no advance access beyond that provided to other journalists.

Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that 76% of Republicans (not 78%) support requiring data center developers to pay for grid upgrades.

item.title: Girls flag football is fastest-growing high school sport
item.description:
Data: NFHS; Map: Brad Jennings/Axios

Girls flag football has become the fastest-growing high school sport, as tens of thousands take up a game that barely had a varsity footprint a few years ago.

Why it matters: Few girls high school sports have moved from niche to mainstream so quickly, broadening athletic opportunities in the process.

By the numbers: More than 102,000 girls played high school flag football in 2025-26, a 551% increase in the past four years, according to the National Federation of State High School Associations.

Catch up quick: In 2024, just 12 states sanctioned high school girls flag football, viewed as a safer, more accessible version of America's most popular spectator sport.

  • Today, 23 states plus Washington, D.C., sanction it as an official varsity sport, and 3,990 schools reported participants in 2025-26.

The NFL is backing its growth, too. It has invested millions to launch and expand high school programs, and featured the sport in its Super Bowl commercials.

Beyond high schools, flag football will debut at the 2028 Olympics, and at least 40 NCAA schools already offer it as a collegiate varsity sport.

Reality check: It's not yet clear whether flag football is mostly creating new high school athletes or pulling girls from established sports.

  • A recent Newsday analysis on Long Island found flag participation rising sharply while girls lacrosse, softball and track participation fell.

What we're watching: Girls varsity wrestling is undergoing its own boom.

  • All 50 states now report girls wrestling participation, and 40 state athletic associations hold girls wrestling championships, up from just five about a decade ago.

item.title: AI panic sparks rare bipartisan moment on Capitol Hill
item.description:
Lawmakers who want to regulate AI are doing something unusual as Congress barrels towards a lengthy recess with no tangible solution in sight: They're working across the aisle.

Why it matters: Bipartisanship is increasingly elusive on Capitol Hill of late, but it remains a crucial first step for action in a Senate that requires 60 votes to pass most legislation.

  • The latest example: Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) are pressing congressional leadership for a vote on their bill to establish a federal program to assess and monitor AI systems.
  • "Recent incidents of rogue AI agent swarms hacking into public websites and systems have removed lingering doubts concerning the ability of these agents to wreak havoc on our cyber infrastructure," the pair wrote in a letter first obtained by Axios.
  • "Congress cannot delay legislating to address frontier AI risks much longer. Industry-led evaluations are not enough."

State of play: Several new bipartisan efforts to regulate AI have cropped up in the week since several current and former employees at Anthropic and OpenAI went public with concerns about the existential risks posed by their own products.

  • Reps. Russell Fry (R-S.C.) and Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) are founding a caucus focused on AI small businesses, called the Innovators Caucus, as Axios reported Monday.
  • Among the group's stated goals is starting work on a federal framework to regulate AI, as well as bringing small businesses to the AI policymaking table.

The doomsday warnings have also breathed new life into existing bipartisan proposals to mitigate the dangers of AI.

  • Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) has been publicly hawking his bill with Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) to require AI companies to include a human-activated "kill switch" in their systems.
  • Lieu has also privately pitched Democratic leadership on creating a bipartisan AI select committee if they retake control of the House next year.
  • Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) have also been championing their comprehensive AI regulation bill, the Frontier Act.

Zoom out: It has been years since Congress passed multiple pieces of truly big bipartisan legislation, and decades since bipartisan lawmaking on marquee issues was a regular practice.

  • The most common moments when cross-party cooperation sees a renaissance on Capitol Hill these days: crises.
  • Consider what got passed in the 117th Congress, on the heels of the Jan. 6 attack and the COVID pandemic: $1.2 trillion in infrastructure spending, a $280 billion semiconductor and research bill and the first major gun safety law in decades, all with bipartisan majorities.

Yes, but: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has signaled that his chamber will not take any action on the AI front before the House leaves for a six-week recess that doesn't end until after Election Day.

  • Johnson said in a CNN interview Sunday that Congress should "not smother American innovation" with overly burdensome AI regulations.
  • President Trump has gone even further in dismissing the urgency of federal AI regulations, writing in a Truth Social post Monday: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX."

What to watch: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has sounded a considerably more dire note on the issue.

  • A potential House Democratic majority next year may be the place where AI regulation finally finds its footing on Capitol Hill.
item.content:encoded:
Lawmakers who want to regulate AI are doing something unusual as Congress barrels towards a lengthy recess with no tangible solution in sight: They're working across the aisle.

Why it matters: Bipartisanship is increasingly elusive on Capitol Hill of late, but it remains a crucial first step for action in a Senate that requires 60 votes to pass most legislation.

  • The latest example: Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) are pressing congressional leadership for a vote on their bill to establish a federal program to assess and monitor AI systems.
  • "Recent incidents of rogue AI agent swarms hacking into public websites and systems have removed lingering doubts concerning the ability of these agents to wreak havoc on our cyber infrastructure," the pair wrote in a letter first obtained by Axios.
  • "Congress cannot delay legislating to address frontier AI risks much longer. Industry-led evaluations are not enough."

State of play: Several new bipartisan efforts to regulate AI have cropped up in the week since several current and former employees at Anthropic and OpenAI went public with concerns about the existential risks posed by their own products.

  • Reps. Russell Fry (R-S.C.) and Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) are founding a caucus focused on AI small businesses, called the Innovators Caucus, as Axios reported Monday.
  • Among the group's stated goals is starting work on a federal framework to regulate AI, as well as bringing small businesses to the AI policymaking table.

The doomsday warnings have also breathed new life into existing bipartisan proposals to mitigate the dangers of AI.

  • Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) has been publicly hawking his bill with Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) to require AI companies to include a human-activated "kill switch" in their systems.
  • Lieu has also privately pitched Democratic leadership on creating a bipartisan AI select committee if they retake control of the House next year.
  • Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) have also been championing their comprehensive AI regulation bill, the Frontier Act.

Zoom out: It has been years since Congress passed multiple pieces of truly big bipartisan legislation, and decades since bipartisan lawmaking on marquee issues was a regular practice.

  • The most common moments when cross-party cooperation sees a renaissance on Capitol Hill these days: crises.
  • Consider what got passed in the 117th Congress, on the heels of the Jan. 6 attack and the COVID pandemic: $1.2 trillion in infrastructure spending, a $280 billion semiconductor and research bill and the first major gun safety law in decades, all with bipartisan majorities.

Yes, but: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has signaled that his chamber will not take any action on the AI front before the House leaves for a six-week recess that doesn't end until after Election Day.

  • Johnson said in a CNN interview Sunday that Congress should "not smother American innovation" with overly burdensome AI regulations.
  • President Trump has gone even further in dismissing the urgency of federal AI regulations, writing in a Truth Social post Monday: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX."

What to watch: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has sounded a considerably more dire note on the issue.

  • A potential House Democratic majority next year may be the place where AI regulation finally finds its footing on Capitol Hill.

item.title: Rep. Chuck Edwards files complaint against House Ethics
item.description:
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) filed a complaint against the top Republican and Democrat on the House Ethics Committee on Tuesday, accusing the lawmakers who investigated him of breaking their own rules.

Why it matters: Edwards is escalating his fight against the committee just two weeks after the House voted 413-2 to censure him over its findings that he violated House rules related to sexual harassment and a hostile workplace.

  • Edwards' complaint asks the Office of Congressional Conduct to investigate Ethics Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) over their handling of his case.
  • The Ethics Committee has previously disputed Edwards' account of the process. When it released its report last month, Guest and DeSaulnier said Edwards had agreed to waive certain procedural steps after reviewing a draft of the report several days earlier.
  • The committee's findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate.

Driving the news: "There was nothing ethical about this process," Edwards said in announcing the complaint.

  • He alleges the committee circumvented its own rules by adopting its final report and recommending his censure before receiving his formal response.
  • Edwards has maintained that his conduct did not violate House rules, though he did apologize to his wife, family, and the two women he allegedly harassed.
  • The committee declined to comment.

Catch up quick: The Ethics report's findings corroborated several anecdotes previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings.

  • He told one staffer that she had "written a complex chapter in my heart" shortly before she was set to leave his office in a three-page handwritten letter previously reported by Axios.
  • Edwards gave the two young female staffers numerous gifts, including jewelry worth over $1,000, as well as "designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners," the Ethics panel found.

What they're saying: "He has no remorse, and now he's trying to turn the tables and say somehow ethics did something wrong," Rep. Teresa Leger- Fernandez (D-NM), the chair of the Democratic Women's Caucus, told Axios.

  • "It just shows you how hard to touch the man is," she added of Edwards.
  • DeSaulnier told Axios he had not yet read Edwards' complaint but was confident the committee followed the proper process.

item.title: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back
item.description:
The Epstein files fight that consumed the House last year is threatening to engulf Republicans all over again.

Why it matters: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is now just one Republican away from having the support he needs to force another politically painful Epstein vote — and he and his allies are hunting for the final GOP signature.

  • Retiring Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) signed Massie's new discharge petition Monday, joining Massie and Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.).
  • Massie and Mace told Axios they're actively targeting retiring Republicans and members in vulnerable districts for the fourth GOP signature that will get them the magic number to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II.
  • Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), one of four Republicans who bucked President Trump and GOP leadership to sign Massie's first Epstein petition last year, told Axios she's considering signing again and has been having conversations with Massie.

The big picture: The push is reviving one of the most disruptive fights of Trump's second term for House Republicans.

  • Last year's Epstein discharge petition became a months-long headache for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and the White House before ultimately securing 218 signatures and forcing the issue onto the House floor. The bill passed with almost unanimous support in the House.
  • The Epstein Files Transparency Act II would enforce and expand the release of remaining files at DOJ.
  • "The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public. In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing," Massie wrote in a statement last month.

Reality check: Even if Massie locks down the Republican support he needs this week, the House is set to leave Washington Thursday until after the November midterms, meaning any potential floor showdown would come post-election.

  • Democrats also still need to provide the remaining signatures needed to reach the 218 required to discharge the bill, though Democratic leadership is encouraging members to sign on.
  • Massie said he views that as just a logistical problem: "I haven't found any Democrat who's against it."

Behind the scenes: Massie and Mace are focusing their recruitment efforts on Republicans who may have less to lose from crossing Trump.

  • "I've got one hero slot left," Massie told Axios.
  • Massie said he's talking to members in districts "where they're polling 10 points down," arguing they can either stay off the petition and risk losing anyway or sign it and make the issue part of their reelection pitch.
  • Mace told Axios she is also "talking to Republicans who are leaving, and some Republican districts that we need to focus in on now."

The intrigue: Boebert could provide the fourth Republican signature, but Massie says he doesn't expect the Republicans who took the political risk last year to do it again.

  • "Anybody who did the first one is not obligated to put their head in the guillotine again," Massie said when asked about Boebert. "I think it's somebody else's turn."
  • "Ralph Norman did it. He's a new one, and I think there are other new ones out there that we can get," he added.

Between the lines: Massie is again accusing Johnson of manipulating the House calendar to deny him the time needed to force a vote.

  • Johnson recently canceled two of the House's three remaining September workweeks.
  • "He got a call from somebody that's above his pay grade that said, 'Take those two days off the calendar. Don't you dare give Massie the runway to get that plane off the ground,'" Massie said.
  • Johnson, after calling Massie "stupid" for suggesting the House would add recess time, then formally moved to cancel session weeks, as Massie had predicted.

item.title: How Ed Sheeran's tour imploded over a geopolitical fight
item.description:
Ed Sheeran's world tour spiraled into chaos this week after one opener was removed, every remaining opening act quit and stadiums threatened to pull the plug on the tour.

Why it matters: The turmoil reveals the power dynamics behind major concert tours, showing how even a global star like Sheeran can be forced to take a back seat on decisions about his own shows.

Driving the news: All four of Sheeran's remaining supporting acts announced Tuesday that they were dropping out.

  • Irish musicians Aaron Rowe and Beoga, as well as Danish band Lukas Graham, said Tuesday they were leaving the tour. Rowe was set to replace Macklemore as the opener for the U.S. shows, AP reports.
  • Finneas, who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, also announced he was exiting the concert series, saying on Instagram that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed."

Catch up quick: The moves came one day after rapper Macklemore, who was scheduled for most of the remaining tour dates, was dropped after using his sets to voice support for Palestinians and condemn the war in Gaza during shows on Sept. 4-5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

  • Macklemore told the MetLife crowd on Sept. 4 that he wanted to do the tour so he could "say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'" His performance included images of war-torn Gaza playing on the video board.
  • The tour's promoters, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone Monday that concert venues threatened to cancel shows unless Macklemore was dropped from the tour after his pro-Palestinian comments.

Zoom in: Macklemore said the decision came after he spoke with Sheeran, alleging that the headliner faced pressure from stadium owners including Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium.

  • According to Macklemore, Sheeran is typically "apolitical" and the recent round of backlash "challenged" him "in a way it never had before."

The other side: Sheeran shared on Instagram Tuesday that the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour came not from him, but from the promoters.

  • "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

Sheeran also wrote on Instagram that he didn't want his Loop Tour drawn into a public discussion around the war in Gaza.

  • "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," Sheeran wrote on IG. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated."
  • He added: "I have my personal views on the devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own personal way."

Zoom out: The turmoil over Sheeran's concert tour raises broader questions about political speech at concerts.

  • As Rolling Stone notes, several stadiums that opposed Macklemore's appearance are publicly owned.
  • One such venue is Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, which faced calls to cancel Ye's shows earlier this year due to his past antisemitic comments.

The bottom line: Sheeran has tried to keep politics off his stage. The fight over Gaza has now made that neutrality difficult to maintain.

item.title: House quashes another Trump impeachment push with Dem help
item.description:
The House voted for the third time in two years to quash a rogue effort by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to impeach President Trump.

Why it matters: As with the last two times, the vote divided House Democrats. Some sided with Green, but others voted "present" or actively helped GOP leadership defeat the effort.

  • Green frustrated his Democratic colleagues by forcing the vote without support from party leadership, with one telling Axios the move was "fucked up."
  • The Texas Democrat defended his attempts to impeach Trump over killings committed by federal immigration officials, calling it a "life and death" matter.

Driving the news: The House voted 232-147 for Republican leadership's measure to table — effectively, kill — Green's motion to force a vote on impeaching Trump, with 47 members voting "present."

Between the lines: Some Democrats who voted with Green privately sneered before the vote that it was a distraction from party messaging on the House's last in-session week before the midterm.

  • Green pushed back by saying the lawmakers who criticized him "don't have the courage to stand up and face me" and challenging them to debate the matter publicly.

item.title: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building
item.description:
The Kennedy Center's board voted Tuesday to close the iconic performing arts center's main building for a renovation project championed by President Trump, multiple outlets reported and a source familiar confirmed to Axios.

Why it matters: Trump's attempts to put his name on the building, which memorializes former President John F. Kennedy, have fueled an ongoing legal and political battle.

  • The decision came hours after a federal judge again said the center could not put Trump's name on the building.

Driving the news: Trump said in a Truth Social post that the renovation "cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name."

  • He said that if the ruling is not in his allies' favor or is not overturned by the Supreme Court, "the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place."

Catch up quick: A resolution from the board, filed in the ongoing legal fight with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over the Center, cited "water intrusion and deterioration of the center's physical plant" that it said "caused a partial ceiling collapse," arguing the safety risk "greatly outweighs any reputational risk associated with closing the main building."

  • A second resolution filed in the case listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name.

Zoom out: The resolution states that without his name on the building, it's "unlikely" Trump "will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building."

  • It listed options for text on the exterior marble beneath the center's name, including "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" or "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump."

Friction point: U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper blocked the center from closing earlier this year, finding that "the Board was derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" and "based its decision on an insufficient, one-sided presentation of information."

  • But in that order, he said his injunction would not prevent "capital repair work," nor would it "categorically prohibit the Board from closing the Center should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion."

Catch up quick: The renovation project would address issues like corrosion and rehabilitating the building's iconic theaters and Grand Foyer, Axios previously reported.

  • The draft resolution proposes sending marquee events offsite, while continuing some programming at the REACH — an indoor–outdoor space.
  • Beyond infrastructure renovations, Trump ally and board member Paolo Zampolli outlined his luxury vision for the space to Axios' Cuneyt Dil, including expanding the outdoor park to create a "concert hub," and building a marina.

What we're watching: For now, those ideas aren't part of the board's resolution — but the center's future under Trump remains in flux, in part because of an ongoing legal challenge to the president's takeover.

  • And while Trump allies position him as the center's financial savior, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales plunged after the board of trustees voted to name the center after him.

Go deeper: Kennedy Center's survival depends on Trump, DOJ says in new filing

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: Scoop: Trump pollster gives GOP a data center survival guide
item.description:
President Trump's longtime pollster is offering Republican candidates a detailed playbook for neutralizing Democratic attacks over AI data centers — down to what language they should and shouldn't use.

Why it matters: Republican strategists say GOP candidates have been all over the map in responding to the backlash to data centers.

  • The goal is to put Republicans on offense after months of playing defense on the issue.

Driving the news: Pollster Tony Fabrizio warns in a two-page memo obtained by Axios that "unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position."

  • Fabrizio specifically advises candidates not to say, "I support building more data centers," warning: "It will be clipped and show up in ads."
  • Instead, he tells Republicans to support AI infrastructure only if developers pay for their own power needs, protect consumers from higher utility bills and safeguard local water and natural resources.

Fabrizio argues that candidates must make clear those conditions are enforceable, rather than voluntary commitments from tech companies.

  • "This converts the candidate from a defender of technology companies into the person imposing rules on them," Fabrizio writes in the memo, which was sent Monday.

Fabrizio offers a three-step script for candidates.

  • First, "validate" voters' concerns about higher utility bills, the power grid and water use.
  • Second, "draw the line" by vowing not to support projects that force families to subsidize them or allow tech companies to harm surrounding communities.
  • Finally, argue that projects should move forward only if companies provide their own power, protect ratepayers and safeguard local water.

"The order matters," Fabrizio writes. "It adopts voters' concerns as the approval standard instead of asking them to set those concerns aside."

Fabrizio warns against generic support for "more data centers," leading with jobs or China, dismissing local concerns or defending individual projects before their costs and resource demands are known.

By the numbers: Fabrizio's polling shows voters are far more receptive to data center construction with conditions than unrestricted development.

  • Sixty-one percent of registered voters favor allowing construction with conditions, compared with 28% who favor prohibiting data centers altogether.
  • His polling also finds voters oppose additional data center construction without conditions by 65% to 24%.

The background: Fabrizio is a central player in Trump's midterm political operation, helping shape the polling and strategy guiding the GOP's campaign to retain control of Congress.

Yes, but: Trump remains an enthusiastic booster of data centers even as Republicans grapple with growing voter concerns about their local impact.

  • "I'm telling you, it's all a hoax. The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy, and it's the oil of the next 20, 25 years," Trump said Monday.

item.title: Trump considered dangerous, corrupt by majority in new poll
item.description:
Data: The Economist/YouGov; Chart: Avery Lotz

A slight majority of registered voters describe President Trump as corrupt and dangerous, a recent poll found, while just 14% say he isn't divisive.

The big picture: Simply put, polling hasn't been pretty for the president — or for his Iran war, tariffs or other top priorities. Still, with the midterms weeks away, Trump has centered himself, making the election a referendum on his presidency.

By the numbers: "Corrupt" (53%) and "dangerous" (51%) led the list of descriptors voters applied to Trump in the Sept. 11-14 The Economist-YouGov poll of 1,461 U.S. registered voters.

  • Those words were followed by "out-of-touch" (47%), "cruel" (46%) and "bold" (45%).
  • Just 18% said they'd use the word "steady" to describe the president.

Worth noting: Democrats are testing an anti-corruption midterm message as Americans' perceptions of government corruption hit a 20-year high, per Gallup's trend, and polls show Americans believe the president has inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency while in office.

  • The results broke sharply by party — 91% of Democrats and 62% of independents said Trump was corrupt, compared with 10% of Republicans.
  • Republicans weren't universally positive: Less than half (49%) said they'd use the word "honest" to describe the president. Just 10% said it didn't describe him, while 41% had no opinion.
  • Similarly, 38% of Republicans said he was steady, while 53% said they had no opinion.

What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars."

  • Ingle also accused Democrats in Congress of failing to stop waste, fraud and abuse in government.

Zoom out: Trump's approval rating ticked up from the lowest point of his political career, recorded last month in Reuters-Ipsos' trend, this month.

  • Some 35% of Americans approved of his performance, up from 33% in the late August poll, per Reuters.

Between the lines: The last thing many Republicans want, Axios' Marc Caputo reports, is for Trump to make the midterms a vote on his popularity (or lack thereof).

  • Still, Trump headlined both nights of the party's midterm convention in Dallas and pledged a $5,000 dividend to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans keep control of Congress — a plan that would cost more than $1 trillion.

Friction point: YouGov's polling found that a majority signaled they believe it's unlikely Trump actually follows through with the idea, which Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has said would require congressional approval.

  • More than four in 10 (41%) said he definitely wouldn't do it, while an additional 16% said he probably wouldn't. More said it was a bad idea (45%) than those who said it was a good idea (38%).

Methodology: This Economist-sponsored poll was taken September 11-14, 2026. Respondents were selected from YouGov's opt-in panel to be representative of adult U.S. citizens, and screened for voter registration. The margin of error is ± 3.3%.

Go deeper: Even some Republican voters sour on Trump

item.title: Massie moves to impeach Pete Hegseth over Iran War
item.description:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran.

Why it matters: The impeachment effort is a long shot in the GOP-controlled Congress, but Massie's resolution is privileged, meaning he can force a full House vote and put Republicans on the record over Hegseth's handling of the Iran war.

  • It's a dramatic escalation in the retiring lawmaker's months-long push to rein in the Trump administration's war powers. Massie did not give GOP leaders a heads-up on his plans.
  • The effort also comes after the House has repeatedly voted on efforts to constrain the administration's military campaign in Iran, including passing war powers resolutions in June and July directing the president to end U.S. hostilities with Tehran.
  • The House is slated to vote Tuesday on another war powers resolution on the Iran war effort.

Driving the news: Massie's resolution accuses Hegseth of carrying out orders to continue operations in Iran despite Congress' constitutional authority over war and its votes seeking to end the conflict.

  • Massie argued Hegseth's actions "frustrated Congress's ability to exercise its most solemn constitutional responsibility" and allowed an "unlawful war" to continue.
  • "In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense," Massie said on the House floor.
  • The eight-article resolution also targets Hegseth over U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, including accusing him of illegally directing the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization.

Zoom out: Hegseth already faced a separate impeachment push from House Democrats, who introduced six articles against him in April that included allegations he waged an unauthorized war against Iran.

What's next: The House will have to take up the legislation within the next two legislative days, but GOP leaders could also move to vote on tabling the resolution instead.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to say that Massie didn't let GOP leaders know in advance about his plans.

item.title: Kennedy Center's attempt to put Trump's name on building blocked again by judge
item.description:
A federal judge ruled Tuesday that the Kennedy Center's latest attempt to put President Trump's name on the performing arts center violated his earlier order blocking its renaming.

The big picture: The order came just before the Kennedy Center's board, now composed of Trump loyalists, is set to weigh shutting down the building for renovations that members argue must include Trump being "appropriately recognized" on the structure.

Driving the news: While Trump allies have argued the latest attempt to recognize Trump does not violate the law, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper said "[l]inguistic gymnastics cannot extricate the Kennedy Center's Board from an operative judicial order or the governing statute it was designed to enforce."

  • Cooper ordered for Trump's name to be removed from the building in May, saying only Congress could change the name of the center that memorializes President John F. Kennedy.
  • The judge blocked the center from putting an inscription that read "renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump" on the main building or renaming the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."
  • Cooper wrote, "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."

Catch up quick: The board voted last month to again add Trump's name to the building to recognize his renovation push in an apparent attempt to circumvent Cooper's prior ruling.

  • The fresh attempt wouldn't change the building's name. Rather, it would put an inscription under the Kennedy Center sign acknowledging Trump and rename the surrounding plaza after him.

Zoom in: A recent draft resolution from the board, filed in federal court by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), stated that "without such appropriate recognition" it's "unlikely" that Trump would "provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building."

  • It proposed several options for "public recognitions" of the president to be placed on the exterior marble beneath the center's name.
  • Cooper noted in his order, however, that "the government offered 'no proof that current or future donations hinge on President Trump's name being on the building'."

What he's saying: Trump argued in a Tuesday Truth Social post that the center "is in a virtual state of collapse" and argued the board knows he's the "only one" who can save it "because I have the ability to raise the money, and the ability to construct — that few others have."

  • The board will meet today, where they could decide to shut the building down.

Go deeper: Kennedy Center could close today. This Trump ally has big ideas.

item.title: Trump turns on the Supreme Court he helped build
item.description:
President Trump lashed out at the Supreme Court on Tuesday after it struck down the president's mail-in voting order Monday night.

Why it matters: The president slammed the justices over rulings they've issued against him this year, suggesting without evidence that the three justices he appointed to the court are being controlled by the left.

What they're saying: "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • "[T]hey are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won't be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal.
  • "It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country's history."
  • "It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court - it will likely cost me dearly for years to come - but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!"

Zoom in: Trump unloaded on the court for striking down his birthright citizenship policy, in which the justices upheld that those born on American soil are citizens.

  • He also slammed their "horrible decision on Tariffs," after they ruled those unlawful earlier this year.
  • "Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America," Trump wrote.

Between the lines: Without naming them, Trump criticized the three justices he appointed: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

  • He explicitly praised Justices Alito and Thomas, who dissented in Monday's mail-in ballot ruling.
  • The Supreme Court could not be immediately reached for comment.

Zoom out: Despite a few blockbuster cases in which the court has ruled against the president's policies, SCOTUS has overwhelmingly ruled in Trump's favor and has taken up a significant number of his administration's cases through its emergency, or "shadow," docket.

  • That has allowed the president to bypass the full briefing and oral argument process and implement policies through litigation more quickly.

Zoom in: The court has become a bit of a lightning rod, with just 33% of Americans approving of the job it's doing — a record low.

  • Threats to the justices are also on the rise, with Justice Elena Kagan telling Congress in July that the court's police force expects a 40% increase in threats this year.
  • Chief Justice John Roberts has previously warned that attacks by "elected officials from across the political spectrum" on federal rulings undermine America's judicial system and can contribute to threats of violence against justices.
  • Kagan said in her testimony that the justices will continue to do their jobs despite the threats as they "believe legally right, adjudicating cases without fear or favor."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.
